components.name: Chardonnay
components.explain:
Chardonnay is a green-skinned grape from Burgundy and the most adaptable white grape in the world. On its own it tastes fairly neutral, so it shows the place and the cellar more than most grapes: lean, chalky and citrus in Chablis, round and nutty in Meursault, riper and creamier in California.

In Champagne it is one of the three main grapes, bringing finesse, citrus and the ability to age; a Champagne made from it alone is a Blanc de Blancs.

At Brennan's it is everywhere: the Leflaive and Fichet Mâcons by the glass, the white Burgundy pages, the Gainey and the California bottles, and inside most of the Champagnes. When a guest says they like Chardonnay, ask whether they mean crisp and unoaked or rich and buttery, then steer.

card.front: Which grape makes white Burgundy and Blanc de Blancs Champagne?
card.back: Chardonnay. It takes on the place and the cellar: crisp and chalky in Chablis, round and nutty in Meursault, creamy in California, and it brings finesse to Champagne.

components.name: Pinot Noir
components.explain:
Pinot Noir is the red grape of Burgundy: thin-skinned, early ripening and hard to grow, which is why it does best in cool places. It makes pale, silky reds that taste of red cherry and raspberry when young and of earth, mushroom and forest floor with age, with gentle tannin and fresh acidity.

It is also the backbone of most Champagne, pressed gently so its white juice runs clear, giving body and red-fruit depth; made alone it is a Blanc de Noirs.

On our list it runs from the Damien Martin Bourgogne and the Jadot Beaune by the glass to Nuits-Saint-Georges, Volnay and Echézeaux, Oregon's Willamette Valley, and the Chavignol rosé. Its light tannin is why it can sit beside fish such as the redfish as well as beef.

card.front: Why can Pinot Noir go with fish as well as meat?
card.back: It is light in tannin with fresh acidity and red fruit, so it does not clash with fish. It is Burgundy's red grape and the backbone of most Champagne.

components.name: Meunier
components.explain:
Meunier, once called Pinot Meunier, is the third grape of Champagne and a relative of Pinot Noir. Its name means miller, from the white down on the underside of its leaves, which looks dusted with flour.

It buds late and ripens early, so it copes with frost in the cooler valleys, above all the Vallée de la Marne. It gives fruity, supple wines that taste of apple and red berries and are ready young, which is why houses use it to make their non-vintage blends open and generous.

Many of our Champagnes, from the Brennan's Essential to Bollinger, Taittinger and Moët, blend it with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and Argyle and Ridgeview grow it too. Krug and Billecart-Salmon are among the houses that speak up for it.

card.front: What does Meunier bring to a Champagne blend?
card.back: Fruit and suppleness: apple and red berry, ready young. The third Champagne grape, a Pinot relative named miller for the floury down on its leaves.

components.name: Riesling
components.explain:
Riesling is Germany's great white grape, and many sommeliers' favourite. It ripens slowly in cool, steep vineyards, keeps a high, racy acidity and gives intense aromas of green apple, lime, peach and, from slate soils, a stony edge; with age it gains honey and a note sommeliers call petrol.

It is made at every level of sweetness, from bone dry to lusciously sweet, and that acidity keeps even the sweetest from tasting heavy. Low alcohol is common in the Mosel.

Our list is unusually rich in it: the off-dry Berres by the glass, Prüm, Egon Müller, Dönnhoff and Keller from Germany, Bründlmayer's dry Heiligenstein from Austria. Its touch of sweetness and acidity make it the classic answer to spice, smoke and the maple on the duck.

card.front: Why is Riesling the answer to spice at Brennan's?
card.back: A touch of sweetness cools heat, and its racy acidity keeps rich food fresh. Germany's great white, made from bone dry to very sweet, low in alcohol in the Mosel.

components.name: Sauvignon Blanc
components.explain:
Sauvignon Blanc is a green-skinned grape at home in the Loire and Bordeaux. Its aroma is loud and fresh: grapefruit, lime, cut grass, green herbs and, from the flinty soils of Sancerre, a smoky, mineral note. It is usually made dry and unoaked to keep that snap.

In Bordeaux it plays a second role, blended with Sémillon. There it lifts the dry whites and the sweet wines of Sauternes, adding acidity and perfume to Sémillon's richness.

At Brennan's you meet it as the crisp Durand by the glass, the Duckhorn half-bottle and Pascal Cotat's Sancerre, and as the minor partner in Yquem, Suduiraut and Gilette. Its acidity and herbs suit raw oysters, salads and anything with lemon.

card.front: What does Sauvignon Blanc taste like, and where is it from?
card.back: Grapefruit, cut grass and herbs, crisp and dry, often with a flinty note. Loire and Bordeaux, where it also lifts Sémillon in sweet Sauternes.

components.name: Chenin Blanc
components.explain:
Chenin Blanc is the white grape of the middle Loire, around Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou. Its acidity is so high that it can be made bone dry, gently sweet, richly sweet or sparkling and still taste fresh, and it ages for decades.

It tastes of quince, pear and apple, with honey, beeswax and chamomile as it ages. In Vouvray the sweetness is printed as sec, demi-sec or moelleux; in the Coteaux du Layon it is usually sweet.

On our list it is Domaine Huet in all three styles, Damien Laureau's Savennières and the Baumard Layon. Tell a guest who fears sweet wine that a demi-sec Chenin tastes of baked apple with a bright finish, never syrupy, which is why it suits the Baked Apple and pork.

card.front: Why can Chenin Blanc be dry, demi-sec or sweet?
card.back: Its acidity is very high, so every style stays fresh. The Loire white of Vouvray, Savennières and Layon: quince, pear and honey, ageing for decades.

components.name: Albariño
components.explain:
Albariño is the white grape of Rías Baixas in Galicia, Spain's rainy Atlantic corner, and of Vinho Verde across the border in Portugal. Its thick skins resist the damp sea air, and vines are often trained high on pergolas so the wind dries them.

It tastes of lemon, white peach and apricot, with a saline snap that seems to come off the ocean. Most is made in steel and bottled young; old vine bottlings and a few years in bottle add texture and a savoury depth.

At Brennan's it is the Pazo das Bruxas by the glass and Do Ferreiro's Cepas Vellas on the list. It is a natural partner for oysters, crab and Gulf fish, just as it is with the seafood of Galicia.

card.front: Where does Albariño come from, and what does it taste like?
card.back: Rías Baixas in Galicia, on the Atlantic: lemon, white peach and a saline, sea-spray snap, usually unoaked. Lovely with oysters, crab and Gulf fish.

components.name: Grüner Veltliner
components.explain:
Grüner Veltliner is Austria's own white grape, about a third of the country's vines, grown along the Danube in the Kamptal, Kremstal and Wachau. Grüner means green.

Its signature is white pepper over green apple, lime and fresh herbs, with a savoury, almost lentil-like note in riper versions. Light ones are crisp and quaffable; old vine and single vineyard wines from the terraces are fuller, textured and long, still dry.

We pour four: Loimer's Lois and Bründlmayer's Terrassen in the light style, Bründlmayer's Alte Reben and Hirtzberger's Honivogl Smaragd in the full one. It is famously good with green vegetables that defeat other wines, such as artichokes and asparagus, and with fried food.

card.front: What is the signature taste of Grüner Veltliner?
card.back: White pepper over green apple, lime and herbs. Austria's own white grape, from light and crisp to full and textured, and good with artichokes and fried food.

components.name: Gamay
components.explain:
Gamay is the red grape of Beaujolais, at the southern end of Burgundy. It makes light, juicy reds, low in tannin and bright in acidity, tasting of red cherry, raspberry, strawberry and violets, sometimes with a peppery edge.

Much of it is made with whole bunches, so fermentation starts inside the uncrushed berries, which keeps the fruit fresh and the tannin soft. The ten crus of Beaujolais, such as Morgon and Fleurie, give deeper wines that can age.

We have Jadot's Beaujolais-Villages half-bottle, Coudert's Fleurie and the two Morgon bottles from Lapierre and Foillard. Gamay takes a light chill and is the friendliest red with spicy, smoky Creole food and with fish, because there is so little tannin to clash.

card.front: Why is Gamay so good with spicy Creole food?
card.back: Very low tannin and bright fruit, so spice does not turn it bitter. The grape of Beaujolais, often made with whole bunches, and happy with a light chill.

components.name: Grenache
components.explain:
Grenache, Garnacha in Spain, is a red grape that loves heat and wind. It ripens late, piles up sugar and gives generous, warm reds that taste of kirsch, strawberry, raspberry and dried herbs, with soft tannin and often high alcohol.

It leads the blends of the Southern Rhône: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas and Côtes du Rhône. It is the base of pale Provence rosé, and in Roussillon it makes the sweet fortified wines of Banyuls and Rivesaltes, where it ages into fig, caramel and coffee.

On our list it is the Durban by the glass, the Gigondas and Châteauneuf bottles, Minuty and Whispering Angel, and the La Tour Vieille Banyuls with dessert. With chocolate, the Banyuls is a famous match.

card.front: Name three very different wines on our list built on Grenache.
card.back: Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Gigondas reds, the pale Minuty and Whispering Angel rosés, and the sweet La Tour Vieille Banyuls served with chocolate.

components.name: Syrah
components.explain:
Syrah is the red grape of the Northern Rhône, called Shiraz in Australia. It gives deep colour, firm but ripe tannin and flavours of blackberry, black raspberry and black pepper, with olive, smoke and violet in cooler places.

In the Southern Rhône it is the spice and backbone in Grenache-led blends; on its own it is unusual there, which is what makes the Châteaumar Cuvée Vincent, all Syrah from old vines near Châteauneuf, a talking point.

You meet it in the breakfast tasting's red with the petite filet, in the Durban and Gigondas blends and in all three bottles of Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Its pepper loves beef, lamb and blackened or grilled meat.

card.front: What does Syrah add to a Southern Rhône blend?
card.back: Colour, firm tannin and black pepper spice. Our breakfast tasting red, the Châteaumar Côtes du Rhône, is unusual in being all Syrah.

components.name: Mourvèdre
components.explain:
Mourvèdre, Monastrell in Spain and Mataro in California and Australia, is a late-ripening red grape that needs the hottest sites by the sea. It gives dark, gamey, savoury wines with firm tannin and flavours of blackberry, leather, herbs and earth.

It is the heart of Bandol on the Provençal coast, where the law asks for at least half in the red, and Domaine Tempier made its name championing it. In Châteauneuf-du-Pape it is the third grape of the blend; Beaucastel gives it an unusually large share.

On our list it shapes the Tempier Bandol rosé, the Beaucastel, the Saint Damien Gigondas and the Pegau. It gives rosé more body and grip than the usual Provence pink.

card.front: What does Mourvèdre give Bandol and Beaucastel?
card.back: Dark, savoury, gamey depth and firm tannin. It leads Bandol, where Domaine Tempier championed it, and takes a large share at Beaucastel.

components.name: Cinsault
components.explain:
Cinsault is a southern French red grape with large, juicy berries and thin skins. It gives light, fragrant wine with soft red fruit and floral notes and little tannin, which makes it a favourite for pale rosé.

In Provence it is blended with Grenache for lightness and perfume; in Bandol it softens Mourvèdre; in the Southern Rhône it is one of the permitted grapes of Gigondas and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. In South Africa it is one parent of Pinotage.

On our list it appears in Whispering Angel, the Tempier Bandol rosé and the Saint Damien Gigondas. A server rarely needs to sell Cinsault by name, but knowing it explains why these rosés are so delicate.

card.front: What does Cinsault bring to a Provence rosé?
card.back: Lightness and perfume: soft red fruit, flowers and little tannin. It is blended with Grenache in Whispering Angel and softens Mourvèdre in Bandol.

components.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
components.explain:
Cabernet Sauvignon is the red grape of Bordeaux's Left Bank and of Napa Valley. Small, thick-skinned berries give deep colour, firm tannin and flavours of blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and graphite, with a fresh, structured frame that ages for decades.

It is born of a chance crossing of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, and in Bordeaux it is blended with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot. In California it is often bottled almost alone.

Ours run from the Moulin d'Issan by the glass and the dinner tasting's Paul Hobbs Coombsville to Inglenook Rubicon, Ridge's mountain Estate, Duckhorn and the Pauillac and Saint-Julien growths. Its tannin loves fat and protein: filet, Chateaubriand and hanger steak.

card.front: Why is Cabernet Sauvignon the steak wine?
card.back: Firm tannin meets the fat and protein of beef, and blackcurrant and cedar stand up to it. The grape of Bordeaux's Left Bank and Napa.

components.name: Merlot
components.explain:
Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape. It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon and gives rounder, plusher wine: plum, black cherry, cocoa and soft tannin.

On the Right Bank, in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, it leads the blend on clay and limestone. On the Left Bank it fills out Cabernet Sauvignon, and Pichon Lalande is known for using more of it than its Pauillac neighbours. In California Duckhorn first made its name with Merlot.

On our list it is in the Moulin d'Issan, Troplong Mondot, the Médoc growths, Inglenook Rubicon and Duckhorn's Cabernet. For a guest who wants red but finds Cabernet too firm, a Merlot-led Saint-Émilion is the gentle step.

card.front: How is Merlot different from Cabernet Sauvignon?
card.back: Rounder and plusher: plum, black cherry and cocoa with softer tannin, ripening earlier. It leads Right Bank Saint-Émilion and softens Left Bank blends.

components.name: Cabernet Franc
components.explain:
Cabernet Franc is the parent of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. It is lighter in body, with red fruit, violets, graphite and a leafy, herbal note, and fine tannin.

In Bordeaux it is a blending partner, important in Saint-Émilion, where it gives perfume and freshness. In the Loire it stars alone in Chinon and Saumur-Champigny. Because it buds and ripens early and its wood withstands cold, it grows in Canada, where Inniskillin even makes it into a rare red icewine.

On our list it is in the Troplong Mondot, Pichon Lalande, Inglenook Rubicon and the Duckhorn, and it is the whole of the Inniskillin icewine, which tastes of strawberry and rhubarb.

card.front: What is unusual about our Inniskillin icewine?
card.back: It is red, made from Cabernet Franc, picked frozen in a Canadian winter. Elsewhere Cabernet Franc is a perfumed partner in Bordeaux blends such as Saint-Émilion.

components.name: Barbera
components.explain:
Barbera is the everyday red grape of Piemonte in north-west Italy, grown around Asti and Alba. Unusually for a red, it has high acidity and low tannin, so it tastes juicy and bright: dark cherry, plum and a little spice.

Piemontese families drink it at the table while their Barolo ages, and it is a natural partner for tomato, which shares its acidity. Some are aged in new oak for a richer style; La Miraja describes native fermentation in steel and about a year in neutral oak.

At Brennan's it is the La Miraja Le Masche by the glass. Sell it as the red for tomato and spice: the Creole sauces and the shrimp and grits.

card.front: Why does Barbera love tomato and Creole sauces?
card.back: High acidity and low tannin make it juicy and bright, matching tomato's own acidity. Piemonte's everyday red; ours is La Miraja Le Masche.

components.name: Zinfandel
components.explain:
Zinfandel is California's heritage red grape, the same variety as Primitivo in southern Italy, with roots in Croatia. Gold Rush-era settlers planted it widely, and some vines in Sonoma are well over a century old.

It ripens unevenly, so a bunch can carry raisined and green berries together. It gives brambly blackberry, raspberry, black pepper and sweet spice, often with high alcohol. Old vine Zinfandel is usually a field blend with Petite Sirah and Carignane, as at Ridge's Lytton Springs. Picked very late, it makes sweet wine like Ridge Essence.

We pour Ridge's Lytton Springs, Three Valleys and Essence. Its ripe fruit and pepper handle barbecue, smoke and spice.

card.front: What is Zinfandel, and why does it suit barbecue?
card.back: California's heritage red, the same grape as Italian Primitivo: brambly fruit, pepper and spice handle smoke and sweet sauces. Ridge makes ours.

components.name: Petite Sirah and Carignane
components.explain:
Petite Sirah and Carignane are the two partners Zinfandel grew up with in California's old vineyards. Petite Sirah, a cross of Syrah and an old French grape called Peloursin, is inky and tannic, with blueberry and black pepper. Carignane, Carignan in France, adds bright acidity, red fruit and a rustic spice.

Early growers planted them side by side with Zinfandel as a field blend, picked and fermented together, so the wine was balanced in the vineyard rather than in the cellar. Ridge keeps that tradition, naming each grape on the label.

They give the Ridge Lytton Springs and Three Valleys their colour, grip and freshness. When a guest asks why the bottle says Lytton Springs rather than Zinfandel, the share of each grape changes with the vintage, so the back label or the sommelier has the answer.

card.front: What do Petite Sirah and Carignane add to Ridge's Zinfandel blends?
card.back: Petite Sirah adds inky colour and tannin, Carignane bright acidity and spice. Planted with Zinfandel as an old California field blend.

components.name: Tempranillo and Graciano
components.explain:
Tempranillo is Spain's great red grape; its name comes from temprano, early, because it ripens early. In Rioja it gives medium-bodied wine with red cherry, strawberry, tobacco and leather and moderate tannin, and it takes well to long barrel ageing.

Graciano is a small, aromatic partner, deep in colour and high in acidity, used in a few parts in ten to lift the blend and help it age.

Our La Rioja Alta Gran Reserva 904 is about nine parts Tempranillo to one of Graciano, aged about four years in American oak, which adds vanilla, coconut and sweet spice. It is a mellow, savoury red for lamb, duck and roast meats, and a good bottle for a guest who loves old-style wine.

card.front: What grapes are in the La Rioja Alta 904?
card.back: About nine parts Tempranillo, Spain's early-ripening red, to one of Graciano, which lifts colour and acidity. Aged about four years in American oak.

components.name: Sémillon
components.explain:
Sémillon is a golden-skinned white grape from Bordeaux. Its thin skins make it prone to botrytis, the noble rot that shrivels grapes in autumn mists, and that is what makes it the heart of Sauternes and Barsac.

It gives weight, a waxy, honeyed texture and flavours of apricot, lemon and saffron, while a little Sauvignon Blanc usually adds acidity and perfume. Château Climens is unusual in using Sémillon alone.

Every Sauternes and Barsac on our list is Sémillon-led: Yquem, Suduiraut, Climens and Gilette. With age it turns amber and tastes of crème brûlée and marmalade, which is why it flatters the Bread Pudding and the Bananas Foster.

card.front: Which grape is the heart of Sauternes, and why?
card.back: Sémillon: thin skins invite noble rot, and it gives honeyed weight. A little Sauvignon Blanc adds freshness; Climens uses Sémillon alone.

Château Suduiraut Sauternes Premier Cru Classé 2010

components.name: Melon de Bourgogne
components.explain:
Melon de Bourgogne is the grape of Muscadet, near Nantes, where the Loire meets the Atlantic. As its name says, it came from Burgundy; after a hard frost destroyed the vineyards of the region, growers replanted with this frost-hardy vine.

On its own it is light and neutral, with lemon, green apple and a salty, oyster-shell finish. Growers give it more by leaving it on its lees, the spent yeast, for months or years, which adds texture and a bready, savoury depth.

Our two, from Domaine de l'Écu and Domaine de la Pépière, are serious Muscadet, aged long on the lees. They are the classic wine with raw oysters, and with the Grand Isle Jewels they are hard to beat.

card.front: What is Muscadet made from, and what is it made for?
card.back: Melon de Bourgogne, aged on its lees near Nantes: lemon, green apple and a salty finish. The classic oyster wine.

items: Domaine de la Pépière ‘Monnières-Saint Fiacre’ Muscadet 2020

components.name: Godello
components.explain:
Godello is a white grape of north-west Spain, grown in Valdeorras in Galicia and in Bierzo next door. It was nearly lost in the twentieth century and was revived by a handful of growers.

It gives a white of real weight that stays fresh: lemon, pear, almond and herbs with a saline edge, often textured by time on the lees or in older barrels. Sommeliers compare it to a cross between Chablis and white Burgundy.

Ours is Raúl Pérez's Ultreia from Bierzo. It is a fine choice for a guest who likes white Burgundy and wants something new, and for richer fish and crab.

card.front: How would you describe Godello to a white Burgundy lover?
card.back: A Spanish white of real weight that stays fresh: lemon, pear and almond with a saline edge. Ours is Raúl Pérez's Ultreia from Bierzo.

components.name: Pinot Gris
components.explain:
Pinot Gris is a pink-grey skinned mutation of Pinot Noir. In Italy it is Pinot Grigio, made light and crisp; in Alsace it is a different animal: rich, full and spicy, with ripe pear, quince, honey and a smoky note.

Alsace growers often pick it very ripe, so some bottles carry a touch of sweetness and others are dry; the label does not always say, so the sommelier is the one to ask. It ages well, gaining dried apricot, ginger and mushroom.

We have Albert Boxler's and Trimbach's Réserve Personnelle 2007. Its weight and spice handle rich, smoky dishes, duck and foie gras.

card.front: How is Alsace Pinot Gris different from Pinot Grigio?
card.back: Rich, full and smoky with pear, quince and honey, sometimes a touch sweet, where Pinot Grigio is light and crisp. Ask the sommelier how sweet a bottle is.

components.name: Assyrtiko
components.explain:
Assyrtiko is the great white grape of Santorini. It keeps very high acidity even in the hot, dry Aegean summer, which is rare, and gives bone dry wine tasting of lemon, salt, flint and white flowers.

On Santorini the vines grow in volcanic pumice that phylloxera never reached, so many are ungrafted and very old, trained low into basket shapes against the wind. The result has a savoury, almost salty depth.

Ours is Gaia's Wild Ferment, fermented with the island's own yeasts. Sell it as the white for grilled fish, lemon and herbs, and for any guest who loves Chablis or Sancerre.

card.front: What makes Santorini Assyrtiko taste salty and electric?
card.back: Volcanic soil, old ungrafted basket-trained vines and a grape that keeps high acidity in heat. Ours is Gaia's Wild Ferment.

components.name: Savagnin
components.explain:
Savagnin is an ancient white grape of the Jura, the hills between Burgundy and Switzerland. It is related to Traminer, the parent of Gewürztraminer, but it is not aromatic in the same way: it is firm, high in acidity and savoury.

It is the only grape allowed in Vin Jaune, the yellow wine, which ages for years in barrel under a veil of yeast and tastes of walnut, curry spice and dried apple.

Ours is the Domaine du Pélican Vin Jaune from Arbois. It is a curiosity for adventurous guests, and a famous match for aged Comté cheese, mushrooms and chicken in cream.

card.front: What is the only grape allowed in Vin Jaune?
card.back: Savagnin, an ancient Jura white related to Traminer, firm and savoury. Aged under a veil of yeast it tastes of walnut and curry spice.

items: Domaine du Pélican Vin Jaune Arbois 2016

components.name: Gewürztraminer
components.explain:
Gewürztraminer is the most perfumed white grape of all. Gewürz means spice in German; the pink-skinned grapes smell of lychee, rose petal, ginger and cinnamon, with low acidity and a rich, oily texture.

It is at its best in Alsace, where it is made from dry to sweet. In great years, grapes left late on the vine are made as Vendanges Tardives, late harvest, richer and sweeter.

We pour the Trimbach Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives 2007, and it is in the Grgich Hills Violetta blend. Its spice is a natural echo of baked apple, cinnamon and Creole spice desserts.

card.front: What does Gewürztraminer smell of?
card.back: Lychee, rose petal, ginger and cinnamon: the most perfumed white grape. Our Trimbach is a late harvest, Vendanges Tardives, so it is sweet.

items: Grgich Hills ‘Violetta’ Late Harvest Napa Valley 2012 (375 ml)

components.name: Marsanne, Roussanne and the southern whites
components.explain:
Marsanne and Roussanne are the white grapes of the Rhône. Marsanne gives body, a waxy texture and flavours of almond, pear and honey; Roussanne adds perfume, herbs and freshness. Grenache Blanc and Clairette, two southern whites, add roundness and floral lift.

Together they make full, textured whites that age well, gaining honey and fennel notes, and they suit rich fish and poultry far better than crisp, lean wines do.

Our example is the rare white of Domaine de Trévallon in the Alpilles, Marsanne-led with Roussanne, a little Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette. It is a bottle for a guest who loves white Burgundy and wants something rarer.

card.front: What grapes make the Trévallon white, and what is the style?
card.back: Marsanne-led with Roussanne, Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette: full and textured, apricot, honey, fennel and herbs. A rare Provence white.

components.name: Palomino
components.explain:
Palomino is the white grape of sherry, grown on the bright white albariza chalk around Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda in southern Spain.

As a table wine it is neutral and low in acidity, which is exactly why it suits sherry: it lets the ageing speak. Under a layer of flor yeast it becomes fino or, in the sea air of Sanlúcar, Manzanilla, tasting of green apple, almond, bread dough and salt.

Ours is La Cigarrera Manzanilla in a half-bottle. Serve it well chilled as an aperitif; it is a bold, classic match for oysters, fried seafood and salty snacks.

card.front: Which grape makes Manzanilla, and why does it work?
card.back: Palomino, grown on white chalk near Jerez. It is neutral, so the flor yeast and sea air of Sanlúcar give the flavour: apple, almond, bread and salt.

items: La Cigarrera Manzanilla Sanlúcar de Barrameda NV (375 ml)

components.name: Moscato Bianco
components.explain:
Moscato Bianco, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains in France, is one of the oldest grape families and one of the few whose wine smells of the grape itself: orange blossom, peach and grapes.

It makes Moscato d'Asti, the sweet wines of Beaumes-de-Venise, and, in Montalcino, Moscadello, the sweet wine the town was famous for long before Brunello. Picked late, the grapes concentrate their sugar and give honey, apricot and candied orange.

Ours is Castello Banfi's Florus, a late harvest Moscadello di Montalcino, now fifteen years old. Its orange blossom and honey suit fruit tarts and the Tarte Tatin.

card.front: What was Montalcino famous for before Brunello?
card.back: Moscadello, a sweet wine from Moscato Bianco. Ours is Banfi's late harvest Florus: honey, apricot, candied orange and orange blossom.

components.name: Welschriesling
components.explain:
Welschriesling is a white grape of central Europe that, despite the name, is no relation to Riesling. It is grown across Austria, Hungary, Slovenia and Croatia.

Dry, it is light and fresh with green apple and citrus. Its real glory is around the Neusiedlersee in Burgenland, where autumn mist off the lake brings noble rot, and the grape keeps its acidity while the sugar concentrates. Blended with Chardonnay it gives creamy, tropical sweet wines.

Ours is the Kracher Cuvée Auslese, Welschriesling with Chardonnay: pear, quince, mandarin and passion fruit, sweet but fresh. It suits fruit desserts and cheese.

card.front: Is Welschriesling a kind of Riesling?
card.back: No, it is unrelated. In Burgenland it makes fresh sweet wines; our Kracher Cuvée Auslese blends it with Chardonnay for pear, quince and passion fruit.

components.name: Corvina and the Valpolicella grapes
components.explain:
Corvina is the main red grape of Valpolicella, in the hills north of Verona, usually blended with Corvinone and Rondinella. On its own it gives light, cherry-scented red with bright acidity.

Its thick skins are what matter: the grapes can be dried for months after picking without rotting, losing water and concentrating sugar, colour and flavour. That process, appassimento, makes dry Amarone and sweet Recioto.

Our bottle is Giuseppe Quintarelli's Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997, from Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella and other local grapes. With chocolate and the richer desserts it is a rare treat.

card.front: Why can Corvina grapes be dried for months?
card.back: Their thick skins resist rot, so they lose water and concentrate sugar and flavour. That makes Amarone and sweet Recioto, like our Quintarelli 1997.

items: Giuseppe Quintarelli Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997

components.name: Malvasia
components.explain:
Malvasia, Malmsey in English, is an ancient family of grapes found all around the Mediterranean. On the Portuguese island of Madeira it gives the sweetest of the four classic styles, named for the grape.

A Malvasia Madeira must carry a lot of sugar, yet the island's high natural acidity keeps it tangy and alive. Warm ageing in old casks turns it amber and gives coffee, caramel, toffee, orange peel, dried fig and walnut.

Ours is the Broadbent Single Cask Malvasia 2009, in a 500 ml bottle. Opened, Madeira lasts longer than almost any wine. Offer it with the Bread Pudding, nuts and coffee desserts.

card.front: Which Madeira style is sweetest, and what keeps it fresh?
card.back: Malvasia, or Malmsey: rich with coffee, caramel and fig, kept tangy by the island's high natural acidity. Ours is the Broadbent Single Cask.

components.name: The Port grapes
components.explain:
Port is made from a field of native Portuguese red grapes grown on the steep schist terraces of the Douro valley. The five most prized are Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Spain's Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão; old vineyards mix dozens together.

Touriga Nacional gives floral violet aromas, deep colour and firm tannin; Touriga Franca adds perfume and red fruit; Tinta Roriz brings body. The blend is why Port can taste of blackberry, plum, violets and dark chocolate at once.

Every Port on our list, from Dow's and Graham's to Taylor Fladgate, Niepoort, Sandeman and Feist, is a blend of these grapes. Most bottles do not name them, so a guest who asks gets the family, not a recipe.

card.front: What grapes make Port?
card.back: A blend of native Douro reds, led by Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca with Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão: violets, blackberry and plum.

components.name: Champagne, the place
components.explain:
Champagne is a region about ninety miles north-east of Paris, around the cities of Reims and Épernay, and only sparkling wine made there may carry its name. It is one of the coolest places in the world to ripen grapes, so the base wines are tart and light, exactly what a sparkling wine needs.

Under the vines is chalk, which drains well, holds water for dry summers and keeps the wines fresh; the houses age their bottles in miles of chalk cellars beneath the towns. The main districts are the Montagne de Reims, the Côte des Blancs, the Vallée de la Marne and the Côte des Bar to the south.

So when a guest asks for Champagne but means any bubbles, gently say which of ours are Champagne and which are sparkling wine from elsewhere.

card.front: Why can only some of our bubbles be called Champagne?
card.back: Champagne is a place north-east of Paris, around Reims and Épernay. Only sparkling wine from there carries the name; Argyle, Schramsberg and Chapel Down are sparkling wine.

components.name: Montagne de Reims and Bouzy
components.explain:
The Montagne de Reims is the wooded hill between Reims and Épernay, more a plateau than a mountain, ringed with vineyards. It is Pinot Noir country, and its Grand Cru villages, Bouzy, Ambonnay, Verzenay and others, give Champagne power, red-fruit depth and structure.

Bouzy is also famous for still red wine, a little of which is blended into rosé Champagne to give it colour. Tauxières is a Premier Cru village on its southern slope; Merfy lies on the smaller hills north-west of Reims.

On our list the Montagne speaks through Paul Bara's Grand Cru rosé and Pierre Paillard's Les Parcelles, both from Bouzy, through Chartogne-Taillet of Merfy and Bollinger's PNTX20, led by Tauxières. Say Pinot Noir, body and red fruit.

card.front: What does the Montagne de Reims give Champagne?
card.back: Pinot Noir power and red-fruit depth. Its Grand Cru village Bouzy gives our Paul Bara rosé and Pierre Paillard, and red wine for rosé blends.

components.name: Côte des Blancs and Vertus
components.explain:
The Côte des Blancs is the east-facing slope south of Épernay, planted almost entirely with Chardonnay; the name means the slope of the whites. Its chalk is very near the surface, and the wines are taut, citrus, chalky and long-lived.

Its Grand Cru villages, among them Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, are the source of the great Blanc de Blancs. Vertus, at the southern end, is a Premier Cru village and home to several fine family growers.

From here come Larmandier-Bernier's Longitude and Veuve Fourny's Blanc de Blancs and rosé, and the Chardonnay in Pol Roger's vintage Blanc de Blancs. Say lemon, chalk and finesse: these are the Champagnes for oysters and caviar.

card.front: Which grape rules the Côte des Blancs, and what does it taste like?
card.back: Chardonnay: lemon, chalk and finesse. Our Larmandier-Bernier and Veuve Fourny come from Vertus at its southern end; pour them with oysters.

components.name: Aÿ and the Vallée de la Marne
components.explain:
The Vallée de la Marne follows the river west from Épernay. Its cooler, frost-prone slopes suit Meunier, while Aÿ, on the north bank near Épernay, is one of Champagne's most famous Grand Cru villages for Pinot Noir.

Aÿ has been a wine town for centuries and is home to Bollinger. Its neighbour Mareuil-sur-Aÿ is home to Billecart-Salmon, and Tours-sur-Marne, a little upstream, to Laurent-Perrier.

So three of our great houses sit within a few miles of one another on the Marne. When a guest asks where Bollinger comes from, the answer is Aÿ, the Pinot Noir village, and it explains the house's rich, powerful style.

card.front: Which of our Champagne houses sit on the Marne near Aÿ?
card.back: Bollinger in Aÿ, a Grand Cru for Pinot Noir; Billecart-Salmon in Mareuil-sur-Aÿ; Laurent-Perrier in Tours-sur-Marne, a little upstream, all within a few miles.

components.name: The Aube and the Côte des Bar
components.explain:
The Côte des Bar, in the Aube département, is Champagne's southern outpost, closer to Chablis than to Reims. Its soils are Kimmeridgian clay and limestone, like Chablis, rather than the chalk of the north, and the warmer slopes are mostly Pinot Noir.

For a long time its grapes went north to the big houses; today its growers and houses are prized for ripe, fruity, generous Champagne.

Our Drappier half-bottle comes from Urville, in the heart of the Côte des Bar, and is about three parts Pinot Noir. It is a softer, rounder Brut than many, easy at the start of breakfast.

card.front: Where is the Côte des Bar, and which of ours comes from it?
card.back: Champagne's southern outpost in the Aube, near Chablis, mostly Pinot Noir. Our Drappier Carte d'Or half-bottle comes from the village of Urville there.

components.name: Alsace
components.explain:
Alsace is a narrow strip of vineyards on France's eastern edge, between the Vosges mountains and the Rhine, facing Germany. The mountains block the rain, so it is one of the driest, sunniest places in France, yet cool enough for aromatic grapes.

Unlike most of France, Alsace names its wines by grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Muscat. It bottles them in tall, slender flutes, and its towns, Colmar, Ribeauvillé and Riquewihr, look half German, half French, because the region changed hands several times.

On our list are Pierre Sparr's Crémant d'Alsace rosé by the glass, Albert Boxler and Trimbach. Alsace whites, rich and spiced, are a natural match for duck, pork and Creole spice.

card.front: How does Alsace label its wines, unlike most of France?
card.back: By grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris. A dry, sunny strip between the Vosges and the Rhine; ours include Pierre Sparr, Boxler and Trimbach.

components.name: The Loire Valley
components.explain:
The Loire is France's longest river, and its vineyards follow it for hundreds of miles, from Sancerre in the centre of France to Muscadet near the Atlantic at Nantes. It is a cool region of crisp, fresh wines, many of them unoaked.

Each stretch has its own grape: Sauvignon Blanc upstream in Sancerre; Chenin Blanc in the middle, around Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou; Cabernet Franc for reds; Melon de Bourgogne for Muscadet by the sea.

Our Loire bottles show the range: the Durand Sauvignon by the glass, Cotat's Sancerre and Chavignol rosé, Huet's Vouvray in three sweetness levels, Laureau's Savennières, the Baumard Layon and two serious Muscadet bottles. Loire wines, high in acidity, suit seafood and light dishes.

card.front: Name the main grapes of the Loire, from Sancerre to the sea.
card.back: Sauvignon Blanc in Sancerre, Chenin Blanc in Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou, Cabernet Franc for reds, and Melon de Bourgogne in Muscadet near Nantes.

components.name: Sancerre and Chavignol
components.explain:
Sancerre is a hilltop town in the upper Loire, and its wine is the benchmark Sauvignon Blanc: lemon, grass and a flinty, smoky edge. A little red and rosé is made from Pinot Noir.

Chavignol, a village below the town, is famous for its steep chalk slopes, above all Les Monts Damnés, the damned mountains, so steep they are worked by hand, and for the Crottin de Chavignol goat cheese. The Cotat family's wines from here are picked riper than most and age remarkably.

We have Pascal Cotat's Les Monts Damnés Sancerre and his rare Chavignol rosé, bottled by lot rather than vintage. A Sancerre with goat cheese is one of the classic pairings.

card.front: What are Les Monts Damnés?
card.back: The damned mountains: a steep chalk slope above Chavignol in Sancerre, worked by hand. Pascal Cotat's Sauvignon Blanc from there is on our list.

components.name: Vouvray
components.explain:
Vouvray is a village on the north bank of the Loire just east of Tours, in Touraine. Its wines are all Chenin Blanc, grown on clay and flint over tuffeau, the soft white limestone the châteaux of the Loire are built from and into which the cellars are carved.

Vouvray is made dry (sec), gently sweet (demi-sec), sweet (moelleux) and sparkling, and the vintage decides: warm years with noble rot give sweet wines, cool years dry and sparkling ones.

Domaine Huet is its greatest estate, with three vineyards, Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and the Clos du Bourg. We pour its sec, demi-sec and moelleux. Always say the sweetness word on the label to the guest.

card.front: What three sweetness words appear on our Huet Vouvray labels?
card.back: Sec, dry; demi-sec, gently sweet; moelleux, sweet. All Chenin Blanc from Vouvray, near Tours, on chalky tuffeau. Always say the word to the guest.

components.name: Anjou: Savennières and the Coteaux du Layon
components.explain:
Anjou lies west of Touraine around the city of Angers, where the Loire meets several tributaries. Chenin Blanc is king here, in two opposite styles.

Savennières, on the north bank, is a tiny appellation of steep schist slopes making dry, firm, waxy Chenin that tastes of quince, beeswax and chamomile and ages for decades. Across the river, the Coteaux du Layon follows a small tributary whose autumn mists bring noble rot, and the wines are sweet, honeyed and fresh.

We have Damien Laureau's Savennières L'Alliance and the Baumard Clos Sainte Catherine 2006 from the Layon. Same grape, same few miles: one dry for fish, one sweet for dessert.

card.front: Savennières and Coteaux du Layon: same grape, what difference?
card.back: Both Anjou Chenin Blanc. Savennières is dry, firm and waxy; the Coteaux du Layon is sweet, honeyed and fresh, from autumn mists by the river.

components.name: Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine
components.explain:
Muscadet is the westernmost Loire wine, made around Nantes near the Atlantic. Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine, named for two small rivers, is its heartland, and its wine is made from Melon de Bourgogne.

The words sur lie on many labels mean the wine stayed on its lees, the spent yeast, through the winter until bottling, gaining texture and a light spritz. The best growers now bottle crus communaux, named villages such as Monnières-Saint Fiacre, Clisson and Gorges, and leave the wine on its lees for two years or more.

Domaine de l'Écu bottles by the rock beneath the vines, so Orthogneiss is named for an ancient rock; Pépière's Monnières-Saint Fiacre is a cru communal. Both are the oyster wine.

card.front: What does sur lie on a Muscadet label mean?
card.back: The wine stayed on its lees, the spent yeast, until bottling: more texture, a light spritz and savoury depth. Our two Muscadet bottles rest on them far longer than usual.

components.name: Chablis
components.explain:
Chablis is the northernmost part of Burgundy, nearer Champagne than Beaune, and it makes only Chardonnay. Its cool climate and Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of fossilised oyster shells, give lean, crisp, steely wines that taste of lemon, green apple and a chalky, oyster-shell finish.

The tiers run Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru. The seven Grand Crus, Les Preuses among them, sit on one slope facing south-west across the little Serein river.

We have Louis Michel's village Chablis and Montmains Premier Cru, made in steel with no oak, and Dauvissat's Les Preuses Grand Cru. Chablis with oysters is the oldest pairing advice there is.

card.front: What soil gives Chablis its oyster-shell finish?
card.back: Kimmeridgian limestone and clay full of fossil oyster shells. Chablis is northern Burgundy's Chardonnay: lean, crisp and steely, the classic oyster wine.

components.name: The Mâconnais and Pouilly-Fuissé
components.explain:
The Mâconnais is the southern end of Burgundy proper, around the town of Mâcon, a warmer, gentler landscape of rolling hills. Almost all its white is Chardonnay, riper and rounder than the Côte d'Or's and much kinder in price.

Mâcon-Villages wines may add the village name, so Mâcon-Verzé, Mâcon-Igé and Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine name villages. Pouilly-Fuissé, under the dramatic limestone rocks of Solutré and Vergisson, is its finest appellation and gained Premier Cru vineyards in 2020.

Great Côte d'Or estates now farm here: Leflaive at Verzé and the Lafon family at Milly-Lamartine. Our dinner tasting white, the Fichet Château London, comes from Igé. Say: white Burgundy with sunshine.

card.front: What do Verzé, Igé and Milly-Lamartine have in common on our list?
card.back: They are Mâconnais villages that name our Mâcon whites: Leflaive's Verzé, Fichet's Château London from Igé and the Lafon family's Milly-Lamartine.

components.name: The Côte de Beaune
components.explain:
The Côte de Beaune is the southern half of the Côte d'Or, the narrow limestone escarpment at the heart of Burgundy, running south from the town of Beaune. It is the home of the greatest white Burgundy, and of silky reds too.

Its white villages, Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet and the hillside Saint-Aubin, share the Grand Cru Le Montrachet. Its red villages include Volnay, known for perfume, Beaune itself, Savigny-lès-Beaune and Pommard.

On our list it gives the Jadot Beaune Premier Cru on the dinner tasting, the Bouchard Clos de la Mousse, d'Angerville's Volnay, Tollot-Beaut's Savigny, and the whole run of Meursault, Puligny and Saint-Aubin. Say elegance: silky reds, rich but precise whites.

card.front: Name four Côte de Beaune villages on our list.
card.back: Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet for white, Volnay and Beaune for red; also Saint-Aubin and Savigny-lès-Beaune. The southern half of the Côte d'Or.

components.name: Meursault
components.explain:
Meursault is the largest white wine village of the Côte de Beaune, and its Chardonnay is the richest of the great three: round, nutty and buttery, with hazelnut, ripe lemon, toast and a stony freshness underneath, usually from fermentation and ageing in oak barrels.

It has no Grand Cru, but famous Premier Crus such as Perrières, Charmes and Genevrières, and many named village vineyards, lieux-dits, like Les Tillets, Les Corbins and the Clos de la Baronne. Every November the village holds the Paulée de Meursault, a harvest feast.

Our list carries Meursault from Jadot, Dupont-Fahn, Bitouzet-Prieur, Comtes Lafon and Leflaive's Sous le Dos d'Ane. For a guest who wants a rich, classic white with lobster or crab, this is the page.

card.front: How does Meursault taste compared with Puligny-Montrachet?
card.back: Meursault is rounder and nuttier, hazelnut and butter over a stony core; Puligny is more chiselled and floral. Both are great Côte de Beaune Chardonnay.

components.name: Puligny-Montrachet and Saint-Aubin
components.explain:
Puligny-Montrachet is the most famous white wine village in the world. It shares with Chassagne the Grand Cru Le Montrachet, and its own Grand Crus and Premier Crus give Chardonnay that is elegant, floral and chiselled: citrus, white flowers, hazelnut and a fine, chalky tension.

The water table is high here, so cellars are shallow and wines are often aged above ground. Saint-Aubin, tucked into the hills behind Puligny and Chassagne, makes wines in a similar style at a gentler price.

We have village Puligny from François Carillon and Domaine Leflaive, and Paul Pillot's Le Charmois Saint-Aubin Premier Cru. Recommend Saint-Aubin to a guest who loves Puligny but wants value.

card.front: Which village is our value alternative to Puligny-Montrachet?
card.back: Saint-Aubin, in the hills behind Puligny and Chassagne, in a similar elegant, chalky style: our Paul Pillot Le Charmois Premier Cru.

items: Domaine Paul Pillot ‘Le Charmois’ Saint-Aubin Premier Cru 2022
Domaine Leflaive ‘Sous le Dos d’Ane’ Meursault Premier Cru 2017

components.name: Beaune
components.explain:
Beaune is the wine capital of Burgundy, a walled town of négociant cellars, home to houses such as Louis Jadot and Bouchard Père & Fils and to the Hospices de Beaune, whose charity wine auction each November is the most famous in France.

Its own vineyards, on the slope above the town, are mostly red Pinot Noir. Beaune has no Grand Cru, so its Premier Crus are its highest tier; they give silky, generous reds with red cherry, raspberry and a little spice, often walled clos such as the Clos de la Mousse and the Clos des Ursules.

Our dinner tasting pours the Jadot Beaune Premier Cru with the Redfish Véronique, and the Bouchard Clos de la Mousse is on the half-bottle list.

card.front: What is the highest vineyard tier in Beaune?
card.back: Premier Cru: Beaune has no Grand Cru. Our Jadot Beaune Premier Cru pours with the Redfish Véronique on the dinner tasting.

items: Bouchard Père & Fils ‘Clos de la Mousse’ Beaune Premier Cru 2022 (375 ml)

components.name: The Côte de Nuits
components.explain:
The Côte de Nuits is the northern half of the Côte d'Or, running from near Dijon south to Nuits-Saint-Georges. It is almost all Pinot Noir and home to nearly all of Burgundy's red Grand Crus: Chambertin, Musigny, Clos de Vougeot, Echézeaux, Romanée-Conti.

Its villages each have a voice: Gevrey-Chambertin for power, Chambolle-Musigny for perfume, Vosne-Romanée for silk and spice, Morey-Saint-Denis between them, Nuits-Saint-Georges for firm, earthy structure.

On our list are Gouges and Grivot from Nuits-Saint-Georges, Roumier's Clos de la Bussière in Morey, Grivot's Echézeaux Grand Cru and Faiveley's Bourgogne from a Nuits house. Say depth and structure: the reds for beef and game.

card.front: How does the Côte de Nuits differ from the Côte de Beaune?
card.back: It is the northern half, almost all Pinot Noir and home to most red Grand Crus: deeper, more structured reds, where the Côte de Beaune is famed for white.

items: Domaine Henri Gouges ‘Les Pruliers’ Nuits-Saint-Georges Premier Cru 2016
Domaine Georges Roumier ‘Clos de la Bussière’ Morey-Saint-Denis Premier Cru 2014
Domaine Jean Grivot Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011

components.name: Nuits-Saint-Georges
components.explain:
Nuits-Saint-Georges is the town that gives the Côte de Nuits its name. Its Pinot Noir is the sturdiest of the Côte: dark cherry and plum, earth, an iron or gamey note and firm tannin for Burgundy, needing a few years to soften.

It has no Grand Cru but many Premier Crus, including Les Saint-Georges and Les Pruliers on the south side of the town. The town is also a centre of the Burgundy trade, home to houses such as Faiveley.

We pour Henri Gouges, the reference name of the village, in a village half-bottle and Les Pruliers Premier Cru, and Grivot's Les Charmois. With the filet, the short rib or game, a Nuits-Saint-Georges is the Burgundy with the backbone.

card.front: What is the style of Nuits-Saint-Georges red?
card.back: The sturdiest Côte de Nuits Pinot: dark cherry, earth and iron, firm tannin. Henri Gouges is its reference grower; Faiveley is based there.

items: Domaine Henri Gouges ‘Les Pruliers’ Nuits-Saint-Georges Premier Cru 2016

components.name: Vosne-Romanée and Echézeaux
components.explain:
Vosne-Romanée is the most celebrated red wine village in Burgundy, home to Romanée-Conti, La Tâche and Richebourg. Its Pinot Noir is silky, spiced and perfumed: dark cherry, rose and baking spice.

Echézeaux is a large Grand Cru just above the Clos de Vougeot, legally within the commune of Flagey-Echézeaux but sold as part of Vosne. Its wines are generous and fragrant, the friendliest entry to Vosne's Grand Crus.

Domaine Jean Grivot is a family domaine of Vosne-Romanée. We have its Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011, now fifteen years old and coming into forest floor, and its Nuits-Saint-Georges Les Charmois. This is a splurge bottle for a guest who knows Burgundy.

card.front: What is our Grand Cru red Burgundy from Vosne-Romanée?
card.back: Domaine Jean Grivot Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011: silky dark cherry, rose and spice, with forest floor from age. Echézeaux sits above the Clos de Vougeot.

items: Domaine Jean Grivot Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011

components.name: Bourgogne: the regional wines
components.explain:
Bourgogne is French for Burgundy, and on a label it marks the regional tier: wine from anywhere in the region, or from vineyards just outside the village boundaries. Bourgogne Rouge is Pinot Noir; Bourgogne Blanc is Chardonnay.

From a good grower these are the best value in Burgundy, often from vines next to famous villages and made exactly like the grander wines, just lighter and ready sooner.

We have four: the Damien Martin Pinot Noir by the glass, Faiveley's Bourgogne Rouge, and Bourgogne Blanc from two Meursault growers, Matrot and Jean-Philippe Fichet. Tell a guest: white Burgundy with a Meursault accent, or red Burgundy at its plainest and freshest.

card.front: What does Bourgogne alone on a label mean?
card.back: The regional tier of Burgundy: Pinot Noir if red, Chardonnay if white. From good growers like Matrot or Fichet, the best value in Burgundy.

items: Thierry et Pascale Matrot Bourgogne Blanc 2022 (375 ml)

components.name: Beaujolais and its ten crus
components.explain:
Beaujolais lies south of the Mâconnais, a land of granite hills planted almost entirely with Gamay. Most of it makes light, fruity red to drink young; Beaujolais-Villages comes from the better villages in the north.

At the top are ten crus, villages that put only their own name on the label: Morgon, Fleurie, Moulin-à-Vent, Brouilly, Chiroubles and five more. Fleurie is known for floral grace; Morgon, and above all its Côte du Py hill of crumbling rock, for depth and grip.

We pour Jadot's Beaujolais-Villages half-bottle, Coudert's Clos de la Roilette Fleurie and the two Morgon bottles from Lapierre and Foillard. A guest who says they do not like Beaujolais usually means the nouveau; a cru is another wine.

card.front: What is a cru Beaujolais, and which do we pour?
card.back: One of ten top villages that label with their own name. We pour Fleurie from Coudert and Morgon from Lapierre and Foillard.

items: Domaine Coudert ‘Clos de la Roilette’ Fleurie 2023

components.name: The Southern Rhône and Côtes du Rhône
components.explain:
The Southern Rhône is the wide, sunny valley around Orange and Avignon, swept by the mistral wind. Its reds are blends led by Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and others, and taste of ripe red fruit, pepper and garrigue, the wild thyme, rosemary and lavender of the hillsides.

Côtes du Rhône is the broad regional name; above it come the villages, such as Beaumes-de-Venise, Gigondas and Vacqueyras, and at the top Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

We pour the Châteaumar Côtes du Rhône on the breakfast tasting, the Durban by the glass, and Gigondas and Châteauneuf by the bottle. Warm, spicy and generous, these are the reds for the filet, lamb and blackened dishes.

card.front: What is garrigue, and where do you taste it?
card.back: The wild thyme, rosemary and lavender of the southern French hills; you taste it in Southern Rhône reds like our Côtes du Rhône, Gigondas and Châteauneuf.

items: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône 2023
Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe ‘La Crau’ Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2014

components.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
components.explain:
Châteauneuf-du-Pape, the Pope's new castle, is named for the summer castle of the popes who lived at nearby Avignon in the fourteenth century. It became one of the first French appellations, with rules written in the 1920s and 1930s.

Thirteen grape varieties are allowed, red and white; most wines are Grenache-led with Syrah and Mourvèdre. Many vineyards are covered in large round stones, galets roulés, which store the day's heat. Bottles carry the papal keys and tiara embossed on the glass.

Our three tell three stories: Pegau's traditional Cuvée Réservée, Beaucastel's Mourvèdre-rich Oenothèque 2007 and Vieux Télégraphe's La Crau 2014. Decant and sell with beef and lamb.

card.front: What does Châteauneuf-du-Pape mean, and how many grapes are allowed?
card.back: The Pope's new castle, after the papal summer castle near Avignon. Thirteen varieties are allowed; most wines, like our Pegau, are Grenache-led.

items: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe ‘La Crau’ Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2014

components.name: Gigondas and Beaumes-de-Venise
components.explain:
Gigondas and Beaumes-de-Venise are neighbouring villages under the Dentelles de Montmirail, a jagged limestone ridge whose name means the lace of Montmirail.

Gigondas makes powerful, Grenache-led reds with Syrah and Mourvèdre, from terraces rising up the slopes: ripe red and black cherry, garrigue, pepper and firm tannin, often called a junior Châteauneuf. Beaumes-de-Venise is famous for its sweet Muscat, but its dry red, Grenache and Syrah, is lighter and juicy.

We pour Domaine de Durban's red by the glass, and Gigondas from Raspail-Ay in a half-bottle and Saint Damien's La Louisianne. Say: the value step to Châteauneuf.

card.front: Why is Gigondas called the value step to Châteauneuf?
card.back: Neighbouring Grenache-led reds with Syrah and Mourvèdre, powerful and spicy, at a gentler price. It sits under the Dentelles de Montmirail.

components.name: Côtes de Provence and pale rosé
components.explain:
Provence, between the Rhône and the Riviera, has made wine since ancient Greek settlers founded Marseille, and today it is the world's reference for pale, dry rosé. Côtes de Provence is its largest appellation.

The wines are mostly Grenache with Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Rolle, Vermentino in Italy, a white grape that adds freshness. The palest colour comes from pressing the grapes gently and quickly, so the juice barely touches the skins.

Our two are Minuty Prestige by the glass, from above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, and Whispering Angel by the bottle. Peach, strawberry and citrus, dry and light: rosé for the courtyard and for Gulf seafood.

card.front: How does a Provence rosé get its pale colour?
card.back: Gentle, quick pressing so the juice barely touches the red skins. Mostly Grenache, Cinsault and Rolle; ours are Minuty and Whispering Angel.

items: Château d’Esclans ‘Whispering Angel’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024

components.name: Bandol
components.explain:
Bandol is a small appellation on the Provençal coast between Marseille and Toulon, with terraced slopes in an amphitheatre facing the sea. It is the home of Mourvèdre, which needs this heat and sea light to ripen.

Its reds must be at least half Mourvèdre and are aged at least eighteen months in wood, dark, gamey and long-lived. Its rosé, Mourvèdre with Grenache and Cinsault, is the most serious in Provence: salmon-pink, savoury and structured, with garrigue and blood orange.

Lucien Peyraud of Domaine Tempier helped make Bandol its own appellation in 1941. We pour the Tempier Bandol rosé, the rosé for a guest who wants pink with real substance.

card.front: What makes Bandol rosé more serious than most?
card.back: Mourvèdre leads it, with Grenache and Cinsault: savoury, structured and salmon-pink. Domaine Tempier, the rosé we pour, helped found the appellation in 1941.

components.name: The Alpilles and Les Baux
components.explain:
The Alpilles are a small range of limestone hills in western Provence, near Saint-Rémy and the hilltop village of Les Baux, a land of olives, wild herbs and vineyards scented with garrigue.

The local appellation, Les Baux-de-Provence, has rules about grapes, and some growers chose to work outside them. Domaine de Trévallon famously planted a blend the rules did not allow, so it labels its wines with the wider regional name, Alpilles, rather than the appellation; they are among the most sought-after wines of the south.

Ours is the rare Trévallon Blanc 2016, Marsanne-led, rich with apricot, honey, fennel and herbs. Sell it as a collector's white.

card.front: Why is Trévallon labelled Alpilles, not an appellation?
card.back: Its grape blend falls outside the local appellation rules, so it uses the regional name. Our Trévallon Blanc 2016 is a rare, collector's white.

components.name: Roussillon: Banyuls and Rivesaltes
components.explain:
Roussillon is French Catalonia, the hot corner of France against the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean, near Perpignan. It is famous for vins doux naturels, sweet wines fortified during fermentation.

Banyuls comes from steep schist terraces above the fishing port of Banyuls-sur-Mer; it must be at least half Grenache noir. Rivesaltes, from the plain and hills further north, uses Grenache in its three colours and Muscat. Both may age for decades in old casks, often in the sun, turning amber and nutty.

We pour the La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva with the dinner tasting's dessert, and the Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 is on the list: fifty-one years in wood.

card.front: What are Banyuls and Rivesaltes?
card.back: Sweet fortified wines, vins doux naturels, from Roussillon in French Catalonia, mostly Grenache. Our Banyuls pours with dessert; the Riveyrac Rivesaltes is a 1975.

items: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV

components.name: The Jura and Arbois
components.explain:
The Jura is a small, cool, hilly region between Burgundy and Switzerland, with its own grapes and traditions. Arbois is its main wine town, and it is also where Louis Pasteur grew up and did his research on fermentation.

Its whites, from Chardonnay and Savagnin, are made either topped up in the usual way or deliberately left under a veil of yeast, which gives a nutty, savoury, sherry-like tang. The most famous is Vin Jaune, which ages over six years and is sold in a squat 62 cl bottle, the clavelin.

Domaine du Pélican is the Arbois estate founded by the d'Angerville family of Volnay. Our bottle is its Vin Jaune 2016.

card.front: What is special about the Jura's Vin Jaune bottle?
card.back: It is a squat 62 cl clavelin, said to be what remains of a litre after six years of ageing under yeast. Ours is Domaine du Pélican from Arbois.

items: Domaine du Pélican Vin Jaune Arbois 2016

components.name: The Médoc and the Left Bank
components.explain:
The Médoc is the long gravel peninsula north of the city of Bordeaux, on the left bank of the Gironde estuary. Its deep, warm gravel drains well and suits Cabernet Sauvignon, which leads the blends with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.

Four villages hold most of the great estates: Margaux, known for perfume; Saint-Julien, for balance; Pauillac, for power, home to three of the five first growths; and Saint-Estèphe, in the north, for firm, earthy structure. Their châteaux were ranked into five growths in 1855.

On our list are Pichon Lalande and Grand-Puy-Lacoste from Pauillac, Talbot from Saint-Julien, La Chapelle de Meyney from Saint-Estèphe, and the Moulin d'Issan from the team at Château d'Issan in Margaux. These are the classic steak reds.

card.front: Name the four great villages of the Médoc and their styles.
card.back: Margaux for perfume, Saint-Julien for balance, Pauillac for power and Saint-Estèphe for firm structure. All Cabernet-led, on gravel by the Gironde.

items: Château Pichon-Longueville Comtesse de Lalande Pauillac 2ème Cru Classé 2004

components.name: Pauillac
components.explain:
Pauillac is the most famous village of the Médoc, home to three of the five first growths, Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild. Its deep gravel ridges give the most powerful, long-lived Cabernet Sauvignon in Bordeaux: blackcurrant, cedar, cigar box and graphite, with firm tannin.

Classic Pauillac smells of what the British trade calls cigar box and pencil shavings, and with age it softens into a long, savoury finish.

We have two: Château Pichon Lalande, a second growth across the road from Latour, with more Merlot than its neighbours, and Grand-Puy-Lacoste, a fifth growth often called one of the best values in the Médoc. With the Chateaubriand, a mature Pauillac is the textbook pairing.

card.front: Which two Pauillac estates do we pour, and how were they ranked in 1855?
card.back: Pichon Lalande, a second growth across the road from Latour, and Grand-Puy-Lacoste, a fifth growth known for value. Powerful, cedar-scented Cabernet.

items: Château Pichon-Longueville Comtesse de Lalande Pauillac 2ème Cru Classé 2004

components.name: Saint-Émilion and the Right Bank
components.explain:
The Right Bank lies east of the Dordogne river, around the medieval hill town of Saint-Émilion and its neighbour Pomerol. Here the soils are clay and limestone, cooler than the Médoc's gravel, and Merlot leads with Cabernet Franc.

The wines are plusher and rounder than the Left Bank's: plum, black cherry, cocoa and a fresh limestone edge, with finer tannin. Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised about every ten years, unlike the fixed 1855 list.

Our bottle is Château Troplong Mondot, on one of the highest points of the Saint-Émilion plateau, in a half-bottle from 2020. Offer it to a guest who wants red Bordeaux that is generous and soft.

card.front: How does Right Bank Bordeaux differ from the Médoc?
card.back: Merlot leads on clay and limestone instead of Cabernet on gravel: plusher plum and cocoa, finer tannin. Ours is Troplong Mondot from Saint-Émilion.

components.name: Margaux and Bordeaux Supérieur
components.explain:
Bordeaux Supérieur is a regional appellation that covers the whole Bordeaux area, with slightly stricter rules than plain Bordeaux: riper grapes and a longer wait before release. It is where great estates often place wine from vineyards outside their village appellation.

Margaux, the most southerly of the Médoc's great villages, is known for perfumed, silky reds. Château d'Issan is one of its oldest estates, a moated castle whose vineyards partly lie on low ground by the estuary that is not entitled to the Margaux name.

Our Moulin d'Issan by the glass is made by the d'Issan team from those vineyards: a Cabernet blend with cassis, plum and cedar, a taste of the Médoc at a glass price.

card.front: Why is Moulin d'Issan a Bordeaux Supérieur, not a Margaux?
card.back: It comes from Château d'Issan vineyards on low ground outside the Margaux appellation. The d'Issan team make it: cassis, plum and cedar by the glass.

components.name: Sauternes and Barsac
components.explain:
Sauternes and Barsac lie about twenty-five miles south of the city of Bordeaux, where the cold little Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne. In autumn the meeting makes morning mist and sunny afternoons, the weather that brings noble rot to Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc and makes some of the world's great sweet wines.

The estates were classified in 1855: Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, then first and second growths. Barsac, on limestone, is a village within Sauternes whose wines may use either name and tend to be a little fresher.

Ours are Yquem, Suduiraut and Gilette from Preignac and Sauternes, and Climens from Barsac. Serve small pours, well chilled, with Bananas Foster, bread pudding or foie gras.

card.front: Why do Sauternes and Barsac make great sweet wine?
card.back: The cold Ciron meets the warm Garonne, giving autumn mist then sun, which brings noble rot. Ours include Yquem, Suduiraut, Gilette and Climens.

items: Château Climens Barsac Premier Cru Classé 2010
Château Suduiraut Sauternes Premier Cru Classé 2010

components.name: The Mosel and the Saar
components.explain:
The Mosel winds through western Germany from the French border to the Rhine at Koblenz, its vineyards on some of the steepest slopes in Europe. The slate soil, blue or red, holds the sun's warmth and gives Riesling a stony, mineral edge.

Mosel Riesling is light, often only 8 to 11 per cent alcohol, with racy acidity and green apple, peach and lime, made from dry to lusciously sweet. The famous villages of the Middle Mosel, Ürzig, Erden and Wehlen, face the sun across the river; the Saar, a cooler tributary, gives the steeliest wines of all, at the Scharzhofberg.

Our Mosel bottles include the Berres and Dr. Hermann by the glass, Stein, Prüm and Egon Müller.

card.front: Why does Mosel Riesling taste so light and stony?
card.back: Steep slate slopes and a cool climate give racy acidity, low alcohol and a mineral edge. Ours include Berres, Dr. Hermann, Prüm and Egon Müller.

items: Dr. Hermann ‘Erdener Prälat’ Riesling Auslese 2014 (375 ml)
J.J. Prüm ‘Wehlener Sonnenuhr’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2015 (1.5 L magnum)
Dr. Hermann ‘Ürziger Würzgarten in der Kranklei’ Riesling Spätlese Goldkapsel 2018

components.name: The Nahe
components.explain:
The Nahe is a small river and wine region between the Mosel and the Rhine, with an unusual patchwork of soils from volcanic rock and porphyry to slate and sandstone, sometimes changing within a single vineyard.

Its Riesling sits between styles: the Mosel's fine acidity with more body and a smoky, stony depth. Niederhausen's Hermannshöhle, beneath a cliff, is called its greatest vineyard; Dönnhoff of Oberhausen is its most famous grower, with the tiny Brücke by the old bridge over the river.

We have two Dönnhoff gold capsule Auslesen and Hexamer's Rheingrafenberg Spätlese from Meddersheim. Sweet but racy, they suit fruit desserts and the Baked Apple.

card.front: Who is the Nahe's most famous grower, and which vineyards do we pour?
card.back: Dönnhoff of Oberhausen: we pour its Oberhäuser Brücke and Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle Auslese Goldkapsel. Hexamer of Meddersheim is our other Nahe grower.

items: Dönnhoff ‘Oberhäuser Brücke’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2023 (375 ml)
Dönnhoff ‘Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2023 (375 ml)

components.name: Rheinhessen
components.explain:
Rheinhessen is Germany's largest wine region, the rolling land inside the bend of the Rhine south of Mainz. For decades it was known for cheap, sweet export wine; since the 1990s a generation of growers has made it one of the most exciting places in Germany.

Its limestone hills, around villages such as Flörsheim-Dalsheim, give Riesling with depth and a stony freshness; dry wines now lead, but great sweet wines are still made in good years.

Weingut Keller of Flörsheim-Dalsheim is the most admired of those growers. Our bottle is its PIUS Auslese, a sweet blend whose varieties change by vintage, in a half-bottle.

card.front: Which Rheinhessen grower do we pour, and what is the wine?
card.back: Weingut Keller of Flörsheim-Dalsheim, among Germany's most admired. Its PIUS Auslese is a sweet blend; the varieties change by vintage.

components.name: The Kamptal and the Wachau
components.explain:
The Kamptal and the Wachau are two of Austria's great white wine valleys along the Danube, west of Vienna. The Wachau is a narrow gorge of steep stone terraces; the Kamptal, following the little Kamp river to the town of Langenlois, is a little wider and warmer.

Both grow Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, dry, on loess and on rock. The Kamptal's Heiligenstein is a famous hill of desert sandstone above Zöbing; the Wachau's Honivogl at Spitz is one of its most famous Grüner sites.

Our Kamptal wines come from Bründlmayer and Loimer of Langenlois; our Wachau bottle is Hirtzberger's Honivogl Smaragd. Say: dry, precise and peppery, with food in mind.

card.front: What do the Kamptal and Wachau grow, and in what style?
card.back: Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, dry, on Danube terraces west of Vienna. Ours are Bründlmayer and Loimer from Langenlois and Hirtzberger from Spitz.

components.name: Burgenland and the Neusiedlersee
components.explain:
Burgenland is Austria's easternmost region, on the Hungarian border. Its heart is the Neusiedlersee, a huge, shallow lake surrounded by reeds and smaller pools.

In autumn, mist rises from the water every morning and the afternoon sun burns it away. That rhythm brings noble rot to the grapes almost every year, which is rare anywhere else, so the village of Illmitz on the eastern shore makes sweet wines that rival Sauternes: Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

Kracher of Illmitz made the region famous for them. Ours is its Cuvée Auslese, Welschriesling with Chardonnay: pear, mandarin and passion fruit, creamy and fresh.

card.front: Why does the Neusiedlersee make sweet wine almost every year?
card.back: Morning mist off the shallow lake and afternoon sun bring noble rot nearly every autumn. Kracher of Illmitz, ours, made the region famous.

components.name: Rías Baixas and Galicia
components.explain:
Rías Baixas is the Atlantic coast of Galicia, in Spain's green north-west corner, named for its rías, long fjord-like inlets where the sea runs deep into the land. It is cool, wet and windy, and famous for seafood: mussels, octopus, oysters and percebes.

Albariño covers almost all the vineyards, often trained high on granite posts to catch the wind and dry the grapes. The Salnés valley, the coolest and most coastal part, gives the most saline, aromatic wines.

Our Pazo das Bruxas by the glass is made by Familia Torres; Do Ferreiro's Cepas Vellas is from very old vines in the Salnés. Lead with them for oysters, crab claws and Gulf fish.

card.front: What are the rías of Rías Baixas?
card.back: Long fjord-like sea inlets on Galicia's Atlantic coast. The cool, salty air gives Albariño its saline snap: our Pazo das Bruxas and Do Ferreiro.

items: Do Ferreiro ‘Cepas Vellas’ Albariño Rías Baixas 2018

components.name: Bierzo
components.explain:
Bierzo is a mountain valley in north-west Spain, in Castilla y León but next to Galicia, on the old pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela. Its climate mixes Atlantic rain and continental heat, on slate and clay slopes.

It was long a forgotten region until the late twentieth century, when a few growers revived its old vines of Mencía for red and Godello for white. Raúl Pérez, born there, is among the best known of them.

Our bottle is his Ultreia Godello; ultreia is an old pilgrims' greeting on the Camino. It is a white of real weight with lemon, pear, almond and a saline edge.

card.front: Where is Bierzo, and what do we pour from it?
card.back: A mountain valley in north-west Spain beside Galicia, on the pilgrim road. We pour Raúl Pérez's Ultreia Godello, a textured, saline white.

components.name: Rioja and Haro
components.explain:
Rioja is Spain's most famous red wine region, along the Ebro river in the north. Rioja Alta, the higher, cooler western part, gives its most elegant wines, and the town of Haro is its historic centre, with a cluster of great bodegas in the Barrio de la Estación, the station quarter, built beside the railway in the late nineteenth century to ship wine to France and beyond.

Rioja is defined by Tempranillo and by ageing: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva mark longer times in barrel and bottle, traditionally American oak.

La Rioja Alta S.A., founded in the station quarter in 1890, makes our Gran Reserva 904.

card.front: What is the station quarter of Haro?
card.back: The cluster of historic Rioja bodegas built beside Haro's railway to ship wine. La Rioja Alta, maker of our 904, was founded there in 1890.

components.name: Jerez and Sanlúcar de Barrameda
components.explain:
Sherry comes from a triangle of towns in Andalucía, southern Spain: Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda. The vineyards are on albariza, a brilliant white chalky soil that holds winter rain through the scorching summer.

Sanlúcar sits at the mouth of the Guadalquivir river, facing the Atlantic. Its cool, humid sea air keeps the flor yeast thick all year, so its fino-style sherry, called Manzanilla, is the lightest and most delicate, with a salty tang only Sanlúcar gives.

La Cigarrera is a family bodega there. Our half-bottle of its Manzanilla is a bold aperitif, chilled, for oysters and fried seafood.

card.front: Why can Manzanilla only come from Sanlúcar de Barrameda?
card.back: The town's cool, humid Atlantic air keeps the flor yeast thick, giving the lightest, saltiest sherry. Ours is La Cigarrera.

components.name: Piemonte and Asti
components.explain:
Piemonte, at the foot of the Alps in north-west Italy, is one of the world's great wine regions. Around Alba it makes Barolo and Barbaresco from Nebbiolo; around Asti, in the hills of the Monferrato, it is known for Barbera and for sweet, sparkling Moscato d'Asti.

Barbera d'Asti is the everyday red of the region: juicy, bright and low in tannin, drunk with every kind of food. The villages, such as Castagnole Monferrato, are crowned with old castles and churches above the vines.

La Miraja works from old castle cellars at Castagnole Monferrato, and its Le Masche Barbera d'Asti is our glass.

card.front: Where does our Barbera come from?
card.back: Asti, in the Monferrato hills of Piemonte. La Miraja works from old castle cellars at Castagnole Monferrato; Le Masche is its Barbera d'Asti.

components.name: Montalcino
components.explain:
Montalcino is a medieval hill town south of Siena in Tuscany, world famous for Brunello di Montalcino, a long-lived red from Sangiovese.

Brunello is in fact the newcomer. For centuries the town's famous wine was Moscadello, a sweet white from Moscato Bianco, praised by Renaissance writers. It almost vanished in the twentieth century and was revived when its own appellation came in 1984.

Castello Banfi, the large estate founded by an American importing family, makes a late harvest Moscadello called Florus. Our bottle is from 2011: a sweet Tuscan rarity with honey, apricot and candied orange.

card.front: Montalcino is famous for Brunello: what came first?
card.back: Moscadello, a sweet white from Moscato Bianco. Castello Banfi's late harvest Florus, on our list, keeps that old tradition alive.

components.name: Valpolicella Classico
components.explain:
Valpolicella is a set of valleys running down from the Lessini mountains to Verona in north-east Italy. The Classico zone, around Negrar, Fumane and San Pietro in Cariano, is the original heart of the region.

It makes four wines from Corvina, Corvinone and Rondinella: light Valpolicella; Ripasso; Amarone, dry and powerful from dried grapes; and Recioto, the oldest of them, sweet from dried grapes. Recioto is thought to be the wine of Roman Verona, and Amarone was born as a Recioto that fermented dry.

Giuseppe Quintarelli worked in the hills above Negrar. Our Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997 is a rare, sweet, velvety red.

card.front: What is Recioto della Valpolicella?
card.back: A sweet red from Corvina and partners dried for months before pressing. The oldest Valpolicella style; ours is Quintarelli's 1997 from Negrar.

items: Giuseppe Quintarelli Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997

components.name: The Douro valley and Porto
components.explain:
The Douro valley in northern Portugal is one of the oldest demarcated wine regions in the world. Its vineyards are carved into terraces on schist slopes above the river, baking hot in summer.

Port is made up the valley at the quintas, the wine estates, then traditionally sent down the river to age in the cool lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across from the city of Porto. The Douro Superior, the far eastern end towards Spain, is hottest and wildest; Taylor Fladgate's Quinta de Vargellas is there.

Many great Port houses were founded by British merchants, which is why so many names are English: Taylor, Graham, Dow, Sandeman. Our list carries Ports from Dow's, Graham's, Taylor Fladgate, Niepoort, Sandeman and Feist.

card.front: Why do so many Port houses have English names?
card.back: British merchants founded many of them to ship Port. The wine grows on Douro schist terraces and ages in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia.
