components.name: Madeira, the island
components.explain:
Madeira is a volcanic Portuguese island in the Atlantic, west of the coast of Morocco. Its wine was the wine of early America: ships called there on the way west, and the barrels were found to improve in the heat of the hold on long voyages.

Today producers recreate that heat on the island, then age the wine for years; once opened, a bottle lasts for months. The four classic grapes name the sweetness: Sercial, driest, then Verdelho, Bual and Malvasia, sweetest.

Our bottle is the Broadbent Single Cask Malvasia 2009, a 500 ml bottle from one cask of one harvest. Its tang and caramel suit the Bread Pudding and nuts.

card.front: Why does Madeira last so long once opened?
card.back: It has already been heated and aged with air for years, so it cannot be spoiled by more. The island's wine was a favourite of early America.

components.name: Napa Valley and Rutherford
components.explain:
Napa Valley is a valley about thirty miles long, north of San Francisco Bay, and America's most famous wine region. Fog from the bay cools its southern end, while the north, around Calistoga, is warmer; mountains on both sides give its hillside wines.

It is above all Cabernet Sauvignon country, and its middle, around Rutherford and Oakville, is the heart of it: Rutherford is famous for a dusty, cocoa-like note growers call Rutherford dust. Napa's reputation was made at the Paris tasting of 1976, when its wines beat top French ones.

Our Napa wines include Inglenook Rubicon from Rutherford, Paul Hobbs from Coombsville, Duckhorn, Montelena, Kongsgaard, Grgich Hills and Schramsberg.

card.front: What is Rutherford dust?
card.back: The dusty, cocoa-like note growers find in Cabernet from Rutherford, in the heart of Napa Valley. Our Inglenook Rubicon comes from there.

components.name: Coombsville
components.explain:
Coombsville is a small district in the south-east corner of Napa Valley, in the hills east of the city of Napa, and one of the valley's cooler corners. Breezes and fog from San Pablo Bay keep temperatures down, and volcanic soils from an ancient caldera drain well.

The result is Cabernet Sauvignon that ripens slowly and evenly, keeping freshness and fine tannin alongside Napa's dark fruit. It became its own American Viticultural Area in 2011, and it is named for Nathan Coombs, who founded the city of Napa.

Our dinner tasting pours the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet with the Rohan duck: dark fruit and cocoa with the freshness of a cool site.

card.front: Why does the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet stay fresh?
card.back: Coombsville is one of Napa's cooler corners, near San Pablo Bay, so Cabernet ripens slowly and keeps freshness. It pours with the Rohan duck.

components.name: Sonoma County and Dry Creek Valley
components.explain:
Sonoma County lies west of Napa, between the Mayacamas mountains and the Pacific, and it is bigger and more varied, from foggy coast to warm inland valleys.

Dry Creek Valley, north-west of Healdsburg, is warm by day and cool at night, with benchland gravel that has grown Zinfandel since the nineteenth century; many of its old field-blend vineyards survive, including Lytton Springs. The Chalk Hill area, in the hills east of Windsor, is known for rich Chardonnay.

Our Sonoma bottles are Ridge's Lytton Springs, Three Valleys and Essence, and the Chalk Hill Chardonnay. Sell Sonoma as California with a little more variety and old-vine character than Napa.

card.front: What is Dry Creek Valley known for?
card.back: Old-vine Zinfandel field blends on warm benchland in Sonoma County, such as Ridge's Lytton Springs on our list, planted from 1901.

components.name: The Santa Cruz Mountains
components.explain:
The Santa Cruz Mountains run along the coast south of San Francisco, with vineyards high on ridges above the fog, some over two thousand feet up. Cool nights, thin soils and fractured limestone give Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay with freshness and structure rather than plush ripeness.

Ridge Vineyards' Monte Bello estate sits near the top of one ridge. Its 1971 Cabernet came fifth among the reds at the Paris tasting of 1976 and won the thirtieth anniversary re-tasting outright in 2006.

Our Ridge Estate Cabernet comes from vineyards around Monte Bello: blackcurrant, cedar and graphite, structured and savoury, in a half-bottle.

card.front: Which Ridge wine won the 2006 re-tasting of the Judgment of Paris?
card.back: Monte Bello 1971, from the Santa Cruz Mountains. Our Ridge Estate Cabernet half-bottle comes from vineyards around Monte Bello, high on the ridge.

components.name: The Sta. Rita Hills
components.explain:
The Sta. Rita Hills are in Santa Barbara County, in the west of the Santa Ynez Valley. The valley runs east to west, unusually for California, so cold Pacific air and fog pour straight in, making it one of the coolest wine areas in the state.

That cool, windy climate gives Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with bright acidity and a lean, Burgundian line. The Sanford & Benedict vineyard, planted in 1971, was its pioneer.

Our wines from here are the Gainey Chardonnay by the glass, Sandhi, and Au Bon Climat's Sanford & Benedict Chardonnay. Sell them as California fruit with Burgundian freshness.

card.front: Why are the Sta. Rita Hills so cool?
card.back: The valley runs east to west, so Pacific fog and wind pour in. Chardonnay keeps bright acidity: our Gainey, Sandhi and Au Bon Climat.

components.name: California's North Coast sparkling
components.explain:
California's North Coast covers Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino and Lake counties. Its coolest corners, near the bay and the ocean, grow Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with the high acidity that sparkling wine needs.

Several producers make sparkling wine there by the traditional method, the same method as Champagne, including second fermentation in bottle and years on the lees. Schramsberg, in the hills of Calistoga, was a pioneer, and its Blanc de Blancs was poured at the Toast to Peace in Beijing in 1972.

On our list are Schramsberg's Blanc de Blancs half-bottle and its Mirabelle rosé, the Louis Pommery rosé from California and Duckhorn's North Coast Sauvignon Blanc. Say sparkling wine, never Champagne.

card.front: What do we call Schramsberg or Mirabelle at the table?
card.back: Sparkling wine, never Champagne: they are made in California by the traditional method. Schramsberg was poured at the 1972 Toast to Peace.

components.name: The Willamette Valley
components.explain:
The Willamette Valley in Oregon runs south from Portland between the Coast Range and the Cascades. Its cool, rainy climate is a cousin of Burgundy's, and since the 1960s it has become America's leading home of Pinot Noir and, increasingly, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

Its hills, such as the Dundee Hills with red volcanic soil and the Eola-Amity Hills, give Pinot Noir with red cherry, cranberry and forest floor, light on its feet and earthy.

We pour Argyle's sparkling wine by the glass, and Bergstrom and Ken Wright Pinot Noir. Say: Burgundy's grape with Oregon's bright fruit.

card.front: Why is the Willamette Valley compared with Burgundy?
card.back: A cool, rainy climate suited to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Our Argyle sparkling, Bergstrom and Ken Wright Pinot Noir come from there.

components.name: English sparkling wine: Kent and Sussex
components.explain:
England's south coast is now a serious sparkling wine region. The chalk of the South Downs and the North Downs in Kent and Sussex is the same seam that surfaces in Champagne, and a warming climate lets Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier ripen just enough to keep high acidity.

The wines are made by the traditional method and taste of green apple, lemon and red currant, bright and fine. Ridgeview at Ditchling in Sussex and Chapel Down at Tenterden in Kent, England's largest producer, are among the best known.

We pour Ridgeview's Bloomsbury and Chapel Down's rosé. They make a fun talking point for a guest who has never tried English wine.

card.front: What links English sparkling wine with Champagne?
card.back: The same chalk seam and the same grapes and method. Ours are Ridgeview Bloomsbury from Sussex and Chapel Down rosé from Kent.

components.name: Santorini
components.explain:
Santorini is the volcanic Greek island in the Aegean whose eruption, more than three thousand years ago, left a flooded caldera and a soil of pumice and ash. There is almost no rain, and fierce winds blow across the island.

Growers train vines low into round baskets, kouloura, which shelter the grapes from wind and sand. Phylloxera never reached the island, so the vines grow on their own roots, many very old.

The great grape is Assyrtiko, bone dry, salty and electric. Ours is Gaia Wines' Wild Ferment, fermented with the island's own yeasts.

card.front: What is a kouloura on Santorini?
card.back: A vine trained low into a round basket to shelter the grapes from fierce wind. The island's Assyrtiko, like our Gaia, grows on its own old roots.

components.name: Kumeu and Auckland
components.explain:
Kumeu is a small district north-west of Auckland, on New Zealand's North Island. It is warmer and more humid than the famous South Island regions, with clay soils, and it has a long history of family wineries founded by immigrants from Croatia.

New Zealand is best known for Sauvignon Blanc from Marlborough, but Kumeu has made its name with Chardonnay in a Burgundian style: citrus, white peach, hazelnut and a fine, mineral finish.

Kumeu River, run by the Brajkovich family, is its leader. We pour its Estate Chardonnay, a smart alternative for a guest who loves white Burgundy.

card.front: What is Kumeu River known for, and from where?
card.back: Burgundian style Chardonnay from Kumeu, near Auckland on New Zealand's North Island, made by the Brajkovich family. Ours is the Estate.

components.name: The Niagara Peninsula
components.explain:
The Niagara Peninsula lies in Ontario, Canada, between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. The lakes temper the climate, and a long escarpment traps the lake air, so vines survive the winter.

Canadian winters are reliably cold enough to freeze grapes on the vine, which makes Niagara one of the world's great sources of icewine: grapes are picked frozen, often at night, and pressed while still frozen, leaving only a few drops of very sweet juice.

Inniskillin, founded at Niagara-on-the-Lake in 1975, put Canadian icewine on the world map. Ours is its rare red icewine from Cabernet Franc.

card.front: Why is Niagara one of the great icewine regions?
card.back: Winters reliably freeze grapes on the vine, while the lakes help vines survive. Inniskillin of Niagara made Canadian icewine famous.

components.name: The traditional method
components.explain:
The traditional method, méthode champenoise in Champagne, is how every Champagne and our best sparkling wines get their bubbles. First a still, dry, tart base wine is made and blended. Then it is bottled with a little sugar and yeast and capped, and a second fermentation happens inside the bottle; the carbon dioxide cannot escape, so it dissolves into the wine.

The dead yeast, the lees, then rests in the bottle for months or years, adding fine bubbles and a brioche, toasty depth. The bottles are turned and tipped neck down, riddling, the frozen plug of yeast is shot out, disgorging, and a final dose of wine and sugar is added before the cork goes in.

Crémant, Argyle, Schramsberg, Mirabelle and the English wines are all made this way; only the place differs.

card.front: Where does the second fermentation happen in the traditional method?
card.back: Inside the bottle the guest is served. The yeast then rests there on its lees, is riddled and disgorged, and a final dose is added.

components.name: Crémant
components.explain:
Crémant is the name for French sparkling wine made by the traditional method outside Champagne, in regions such as Alsace, Burgundy, the Loire and Limoux, in the Languedoc. The rules are strict and close to Champagne's: hand harvesting, gentle whole-bunch pressing, a second fermentation in bottle and at least nine months on the lees.

Each region uses its own grapes. Crémant d'Alsace is often Pinot Blanc, Riesling or Chardonnay, and Crémant d'Alsace rosé must be all Pinot Noir.

Our Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d'Alsace by the glass shows the point: strawberry and red currant, dry, with a creamy mousse, made the same way as Champagne at a friendlier price. Never call it Champagne; call it Crémant, or French sparkling rosé.

card.front: What is a Crémant, and how is ours different from Champagne?
card.back: French sparkling wine made by the traditional method outside Champagne. Our Pierre Sparr is all Pinot Noir from Alsace: same method, different place, gentler price.

components.name: Dosage: Brut, Extra Brut and Demi-Sec
components.explain:
Dosage is the small dose of wine and sugar added to a sparkling wine just before the final cork, after disgorging. It balances the high acidity, and it decides the word on the label.

From driest to sweetest: Brut Nature, no sugar added; Extra Brut, up to 6 grams a litre; Brut, up to 12; then Extra Dry, 12 to 17; Sec, 17 to 32; and Demi-Sec, 32 to 50 grams, noticeably sweet. Confusingly, Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut. Pommery's Nature of 1874 helped turn the world towards dry Champagne, when much of it was very sweet.

Our house Brennan's Essential is Extra Brut, very dry; most of the list is Brut; the Moët Nectar Impérial Rosé and Laurent-Perrier Harmony are Demi-Sec, for dessert.

card.front: Rank Brut, Extra Brut and Demi-Sec from driest to sweetest.
card.back: Extra Brut, up to 6 grams of sugar a litre, is driest; then Brut, up to 12; then Demi-Sec, noticeably sweet. Our house Champagne is Extra Brut.

components.name: Non-vintage blending and reserve wines
components.explain:
Most Champagne is non-vintage, written NV: a blend of several harvests rather than one. In a cool northern region where some years ripen poorly, blending lets a house make the same style every year.

Each year the cellar master tastes dozens or hundreds of base wines from different villages, grapes and years and builds the blend, using reserve wines, older wines kept back from earlier harvests, to add depth and keep the house style steady. Non-vintage Champagne must rest at least fifteen months in bottle before release; good houses wait much longer.

Krug takes this furthest, blending more than a hundred wines from many years, and numbers each edition. Bollinger keeps its reserve wines in magnums. Say: NV means the house style, the same glass every time.

card.front: What does NV on a Champagne mean, and why do houses do it?
card.back: Non-vintage: a blend of several harvests, with reserve wines, so the house style tastes the same each year. It rests at least fifteen months before release.

components.name: Vintage Champagne
components.explain:
A vintage Champagne is made from the grapes of a single year, printed on the label, and houses make one only when the harvest is good enough to stand alone, usually a few times a decade. It must age at least three years before release, and the great ones far longer.

A vintage wine shows the character of its year: the warmth of 2009, the freshness of 2013. Prestige cuvées, such as Rare and Billecart-Salmon's Elisabeth Salmon rosé, are usually vintage wines from the best vineyards with long ageing.

On our list: Rare 2012 by the glass and Rare 2013 by the bottle, Pol Roger Blanc de Blancs 2015, Billecart's Elisabeth Salmon 2009, and from elsewhere Argyle 2022 and Schramsberg's Blanc de Blancs 2021. Always read the vintage on the label.

card.front: When does a Champagne house make a vintage wine?
card.back: Only in a harvest good enough to stand alone. It shows that year's character and ages at least three years; Rare, Pol Roger 2015 and Elisabeth Salmon 2009 are ours.

components.name: Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs
components.say: blahn duh BLAHN; blahn duh NWAHR
components.explain:
Blanc de Blancs means white from whites: a sparkling wine made only from white grapes, in Champagne almost always Chardonnay. It is the leanest, most citrus and chalky style, elegant and long-lived.

Blanc de Noirs means white from blacks: a white sparkling wine made only from the black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier, pressed so gently that the juice runs clear. It is fuller and rounder, with red apple and red berry depth.

Ours: Larmandier-Bernier's Longitude, Pol Roger's vintage, Veuve Fourny and Schramsberg are Blanc de Blancs, ideal with oysters and caviar; Bollinger's PNTX20, all Pinot Noir, is a Blanc de Noirs, ideal with richer dishes.

card.front: What is the difference between Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs?
card.back: Blanc de Blancs is from white grapes, Chardonnay: lean and citrus. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier: fuller.

components.name: How rosé Champagne is made
components.explain:
Rosé Champagne is the only French wine allowed to be made pink by blending red and white wine. Most houses add a little still red wine, usually Pinot Noir from villages such as Bouzy or Aÿ, to the white base before the second fermentation, which gives a reliable colour and red-fruit flavour.

The other way, saignée or maceration, leaves crushed black grapes on their skins for a short time until the juice turns pink. It gives deeper colour and more structure, and is rarer.

Most of our rosés, Moët, Taittinger, Paul Bara, Chartogne-Taillet and Veuve Fourny, use the blending method. Rosé Champagne has a little more body than white, so it suits salmon, duck and the Bananas Foster.

card.front: How do most houses make rosé Champagne pink?
card.back: They blend in a little still red wine, usually Pinot Noir, before the second fermentation. The rarer way leaves black grapes briefly on their skins.

components.name: Ageing on the lees
components.explain:
Lees are the spent yeast cells left after fermentation. Leaving a wine in contact with them, instead of drawing it off, slowly changes it: the cells break down and release compounds that add a creamy texture, roundness and flavours of bread, brioche and toast.

In Champagne and every traditional method wine the lees age inside the bottle, which is where the toasty notes and fine, creamy bubbles come from; the longer, the finer. In Muscadet the wine rests on its lees in tank through the winter, sur lie, and the best for two years or more, gaining body and a savoury depth.

So when a guest asks why a Champagne tastes of brioche, the answer is the lees, not oak or added flavour.

card.front: Why does a Champagne taste of brioche and toast?
card.back: Time on its lees, the spent yeast in the bottle. Muscadet rests on its lees in tank too, for texture and savoury depth.

components.name: Oak in Champagne: Sous Bois
components.explain:
Most Champagne is fermented in steel tanks, which keeps the fruit pure. A few houses ferment some or all of their base wines in oak barrels instead, the old way, which adds roundness, a gentle oxidative richness and a toasty, nutty depth.

Sous Bois means under wood: Billecart-Salmon's Sous Bois has every base wine fermented in oak. Bollinger ferments part of its wine in old barrels, which is one reason its Special Cuvée is so rich and structured; Krug ferments in small old casks too.

Our Billecart-Salmon Sous Bois magnum, labelled for Brennan's 80th anniversary, and the Bollinger Special Cuvée show the style. Say: richer and nuttier, a Champagne for food.

card.front: What does Sous Bois on a Champagne label mean?
card.back: Under wood: the base wines were fermented in oak barrels, giving roundness and a toasty, nutty depth. Our 80th anniversary magnum is Billecart's Sous Bois.

components.name: Barrel fermentation and oak for white wine
components.explain:
Great white Burgundy is usually fermented and aged in small oak barrels, about 228 litres, called pièces. Oak lets in a little air, which rounds the wine, and new barrels add toast, vanilla and spice; most growers use only a share of new oak so the fruit stays in front.

Many also stir the lees in the barrel, bâtonnage, for a creamier texture. The richness of Meursault, the hazelnut of Puligny and the toast of the best California Chardonnay come from this cellar work as much as from the grape.

On our list, Jadot's Meursault, Lafon, Leflaive, Carillon, Pillot, Kongsgaard and Au Bon Climat use barrels; Dauvissat ages part in old oak; the Fichet Château London has only a touch of old oak. Ask a guest whether they like oaky or crisp before you choose.

card.front: Where do the toast and hazelnut in white Burgundy come from?
card.back: Fermentation and ageing in small oak barrels, partly new, and stirring the lees. Ask a guest: oaky and rich, or crisp and unoaked?

components.name: Malolactic conversion: the buttery note
components.explain:
Malolactic conversion is a second, gentle fermentation carried out by bacteria, not yeast. It turns the wine's sharp malic acid, the acid of green apples, into softer lactic acid, the acid of milk.

The wine becomes rounder and less tart, and a by-product called diacetyl can give a buttery note. Almost every red goes through it; for whites it is a choice. Most white Burgundy does, which adds to its creaminess; many crisp whites do not, to keep their snap.

The Chateau Montelena Chardonnay is famous for avoiding it, so it stays bright and restrained, while richer California and Meursault styles embrace it. When a guest asks for a buttery Chardonnay, this is what they mean.

card.front: What makes a Chardonnay taste buttery?
card.back: Malolactic conversion: bacteria turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, sometimes with a buttery note. Montelena avoids it to stay bright.

components.name: Unoaked wine: steel tanks
components.explain:
Stainless steel tanks are sealed, neutral and easy to keep cool, so wine fermented and aged in them keeps its fresh fruit, aroma and acidity, with nothing added by wood.

That is the choice for wines whose charm is freshness: Albariño, Sauvignon Blanc, Grüner Veltliner and many Rieslings. In Chablis, Domaine Louis Michel is known for making every wine in steel, with no oak at all, which shows Chardonnay's lemon and oyster-shell purity.

On our list, the Pazo das Bruxas Albariño, Louis Michel's Chablis and Kracher's Cuvée Auslese are made in steel, and the sommelier can name others. For a guest who says no oak, these are the wines to name first.

card.front: Which Chablis do we pour that never sees oak?
card.back: Domaine Louis Michel makes every wine in steel tanks, keeping Chardonnay pure: lemon, green apple and oyster shell. Steel keeps freshness.

components.name: French and American oak for red wine
components.explain:
Most fine reds spend months or years in oak barrels. The wood lets in a trickle of air, which softens tannin and deepens colour, and new barrels add their own flavour.

French oak, tight-grained, gives subtle cedar, spice and toast; it is the choice of Bordeaux, Burgundy and most Napa Cabernet. American oak, more open-grained, gives sweeter vanilla, coconut and dill, and is traditional in Rioja and for Zinfandel. Large old casks, as at Pegau, add little flavour and simply let the wine breathe.

La Rioja Alta's 904 ages about four years in American oak from its own cooperage; Ridge's Lytton Springs uses American oak; Duckhorn, Talbot and the Bordeaux use French. Vanilla and coconut say American; cedar says French.

card.front: How can you tell French oak from American oak in a red?
card.back: French oak gives subtle cedar, spice and toast; American oak gives sweeter vanilla and coconut, as in our Rioja 904 and Ridge Lytton Springs.

components.name: Whole bunches and carbonic maceration
components.explain:
Most red wine is made from grapes taken off their stems and crushed. In Beaujolais and in some traditional cellars, growers ferment whole bunches instead, stems and all, often uncrushed.

In carbonic maceration the whole bunches sit in a tank filled with carbon dioxide; fermentation begins inside each intact berry, before the skins split. The result is very fruity, perfumed and soft in tannin, with notes of strawberry, cherry and sometimes banana or bubblegum in young wine. Whole bunch fermentation in larger wines adds freshness and spice.

Lapierre, Foillard and Coudert use whole bunches for their Beaujolais; Pegau ferments its Châteauneuf with whole bunches in cement. Say: that is why it tastes so juicy and soft.

card.front: What is carbonic maceration, and which of our wines use whole bunches?
card.back: Whole, uncrushed bunches ferment under carbon dioxide, starting inside each berry: juicy and soft. Lapierre, Foillard and Pegau use whole bunches.

components.name: Native yeast fermentation
components.explain:
Fermentation needs yeast to turn sugar into alcohol. Many wineries add a chosen, cultured yeast for a reliable, clean result. Others rely on native yeasts, the wild ones that live on the grape skins and in the cellar, often called a wild or spontaneous ferment.

Native ferments start slowly and are less predictable, but many growers believe the mix of yeasts adds complexity and a sense of place. It is a key idea of the natural wine movement, which the Beaujolais growers of the Gang of Four helped start.

Gaia's Wild Ferment Assyrtiko is named for it; La Miraja describes native fermentation for Le Masche; Lapierre and Foillard rely on it. Say it plainly: fermented with the grapes' own yeasts.

card.front: What does Gaia's Wild Ferment name mean?
card.back: Fermented with native yeasts, the wild ones from the grape skins and cellar, not added cultured yeast. Many growers believe it adds complexity.

components.name: Making pale rosé: direct pressing
components.explain:
All red grape juice is clear; the colour lives in the skins. To make rosé the winemaker controls how long the juice touches the skins.

For pale Provence rosé, the black grapes are pressed straight away, gently, so the juice picks up only the faintest blush: direct pressing. A short maceration of a few hours before pressing gives a deeper pink and more body. Picking early and keeping the juice cold keeps the freshness.

Minuty and Whispering Angel are pale, direct pressed rosés: peach, strawberry and citrus. The Tempier Bandol rosé and Pascal Cotat's Chavignol rosé have more colour and structure. Colour is a hint, not a promise of sweetness: all four are dry.

card.front: Does a pale rosé mean a sweet rosé?
card.back: No: colour comes from brief skin contact, not sugar. Minuty and Whispering Angel are pale and direct pressed; Tempier is deeper. All four of ours are dry.

components.name: The German Prädikat ladder
components.explain:
German and Austrian quality wines can carry a Prädikat, a word that names how ripe the grapes were at harvest, measured by their sugar. From least to most ripe: Kabinett, Spätlese, late harvest, Auslese, selected bunches, Beerenauslese, selected berries, Trockenbeerenauslese, selected dried berries, and Eiswein, from frozen grapes.

The word describes ripeness at picking, not sweetness in the glass: a Kabinett is usually light and lightly sweet, but can be dry; Auslese and above are usually sweet, the highest often touched by noble rot.

Our ladder runs from Kabinett at Prüm and Egon Müller, through Spätlese at Stein and Hexamer, to Auslese at Dr. Hermann, Dönnhoff, Keller, Prüm and Kracher. Read the word aloud and explain it simply.

card.front: Put Kabinett, Auslese and Spätlese in order of ripeness.
card.back: Kabinett, then Spätlese, late harvest, then Auslese, selected bunches. The words measure ripeness at picking, not sweetness in the glass; Auslese is usually sweet.

components.name: Goldkapsel: the gold capsule
components.explain:
Goldkapsel, gold capsule, is a German grower's signal, not a legal category. A grower bottles a richer, more concentrated selection of the same Prädikat, usually from riper or botrytised berries, and dresses it with a gold foil capsule. A long gold capsule, lange Goldkapsel, marks an even finer selection.

So a Goldkapsel Auslese is richer and sweeter than the same grower's plain Auslese, and usually made in small amounts, often in half-bottles.

Our gold capsule wines are Dönnhoff's two Auslesen from the Brücke and the Hermannshöhle, Prüm's Wehlener Sonnenuhr Auslese in magnum and Dr. Hermann's Würzgarten Kranklei Spätlese. Point to the capsule when you present the bottle.

card.back: A richer, more concentrated selection of the same Prädikat, chosen by the grower; not a legal term. Our Dönnhoff and Prüm Auslesen wear one.

components.name: Off-dry and feinherb
components.explain:
An off-dry wine has a little sugar left in it, enough to taste as a soft roundness but not as dessert. In a high-acid grape like Riesling the acidity balances the sugar, so the wine tastes juicy rather than sweet.

German growers use feinherb, or halbtrocken, for wines just off dry. The Berres Old Vines by the glass carries about twenty grams of sugar a litre at only 11.5 per cent alcohol; Stein's Weihwasser and Palmberg-Terrassen are feinherb.

Off-dry wine is a server's secret weapon with Creole spice, smoke, sweet glazes and the maple on the duck: the touch of sugar cools heat that would make a dry wine taste bitter and hot.

card.front: Why does an off-dry Riesling work with spice?
card.back: A touch of sugar cools the heat, and acidity keeps it juicy. Our Berres has about twenty grams a litre; Stein's feinherb wines are just off dry.

components.name: Noble rot: botrytis
components.explain:
Botrytis cinerea is a mould that, in the right weather, becomes noble rot. It needs misty, humid autumn mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons. The mould pierces the grape skins and the sun dries the berries, which shrivel, losing water while the sugar and acidity concentrate.

The grapes look ruined but make the most luscious sweet wines in the world, tasting of honey, apricot, candied orange, saffron and marmalade. Because the rot spreads unevenly, pickers go through the vineyard many times, taking only the affected berries.

Sauternes and Barsac, Burgenland, the Loire and the highest Prädikat levels in Germany depend on it. On our list: Yquem, Suduiraut, Climens, Gilette, Kracher, Keller and the Grgich Violetta.

card.front: How does noble rot make sweet wine?
card.back: A mould, in misty mornings and sunny afternoons, pierces and shrivels the grapes, concentrating sugar and acidity. It makes Sauternes like Yquem.

components.name: Late harvest and Vendanges Tardives
components.explain:
Late harvest wine is made from grapes left on the vine well after the normal picking date, so they lose water, shrivel a little and concentrate their sugar. Some are also touched by noble rot.

The result is sweet wine with the grape's own flavours deepened: honeyed apricot, baked fruit and spice. In Alsace it is called Vendanges Tardives and is allowed only for the four noble grapes in years ripe enough; in California and Italy it is simply late harvest.

Ours are Trimbach's Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives, Ridge's Essence Zinfandel, the Grgich Hills Violetta and Banfi's Florus Moscadello. Each is made only in years the weather allows.

card.front: What does Vendanges Tardives on an Alsace label mean?
card.back: Late harvest: grapes left on the vine to concentrate sugar, making a sweet wine in ripe years only. Our Trimbach Gewurztraminer is one.

components.name: Icewine
components.explain:
Icewine, Eiswein in German, is made from grapes left on the vine into winter until they freeze solid, usually at about minus eight degrees Celsius. They are picked frozen, often at night, and pressed while still frozen.

The water stays behind as ice in the press, so only a few drops of very sweet, concentrated juice run out; a whole vine may make a single glass. The wine is intensely sweet with vivid acidity.

Canada, with reliably cold winters, makes more than anywhere. Our Inniskillin Cabernet Franc Icewine is a rare red one: strawberry, raspberry, rhubarb and candied fruit. Serve a small, well-chilled pour with fruit desserts or cheesecake.

card.front: Why is icewine so sweet and so rare?
card.back: Grapes freeze on the vine and are pressed frozen, so the water stays as ice and only drops of concentrated juice run out. Ours is Inniskillin's red.

components.name: Appassimento: drying the grapes
components.explain:
Appassimento is the Italian art of drying freshly picked grapes before pressing. In Valpolicella the best bunches are laid on bamboo racks or in shallow crates, or hung, in airy lofts for three or four months over the winter.

The grapes lose much of their water and turn half to raisins, concentrating sugar, colour and flavour. Fermented fully dry they make Amarone; stopped while still sweet they make Recioto.

Giuseppe Quintarelli dried his grapes this way on racks and in crates, and our Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997 is the result: dark cherry, fig, raisin and chocolate, sweet and velvety, with fresh acidity.

card.front: What is appassimento, and which of our wines uses it?
card.back: Drying grapes for months before pressing to concentrate sugar and flavour. Quintarelli's Recioto della Valpolicella 1997 is made this way.

items: Giuseppe Quintarelli Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997

components.name: Fortification: vin doux naturel
components.explain:
A vin doux naturel, naturally sweet wine, is made by stopping fermentation partway by adding neutral grape spirit, a process called mutage. The yeast dies, so the grape's own unfermented sugar stays in the wine, and the alcohol rises to about 15 to 18 per cent. Port is made the same way.

In Roussillon, Banyuls and Rivesaltes are then aged either fresh and fruity, or oxidatively for years in old casks or glass demijohns left out in the sun, turning amber and tasting of fig, walnut, caramel and coffee.

The La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva on the dinner tasting is aged the oxidative way; the Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 has spent decades in old casks. Banyuls with chocolate is the classic match.

card.front: How is a vin doux naturel like Banyuls kept sweet?
card.back: Grape spirit is added mid-fermentation, mutage, so the yeast stops and the grape's sugar stays. Ours are La Tour Vieille Banyuls and Riveyrac 1975.

components.name: How Port is made
components.explain:
Port is made in the Douro by stopping the fermentation of red grapes with grape spirit when about half the sugar has turned to alcohol. The young wine is sweet, strong at about 20 per cent and deeply coloured.

Because fermentation is cut short, the colour and tannin must be pulled from the skins fast, so the grapes are trodden by foot in shallow stone tanks called lagares or worked in modern machines that copy it.

Then the style is set by ageing. Ruby styles, including Late Bottled Vintage and Vintage Port, age briefly in large casks and keep their dark fruit; tawny styles age for years in small casks, turning amber and nutty. Our list carries every kind.

card.front: How is Port made sweet and strong?
card.back: Grape spirit stops the fermentation when about half the sugar remains, leaving it sweet at about 20 per cent alcohol. Ageing then decides ruby or tawny.

components.name: Vintage Port and the declaration
components.explain:
Vintage Port is made only in the best years, when a house declares a vintage, usually about three times a decade. The wine spends only about two years in cask, then is bottled young, unfiltered, to age for decades in bottle.

It throws a heavy crust of sediment, so it must stand upright before service and be decanted. Young, it is dense blackberry and chocolate; with age it becomes dried cherry, fig, spice and cedar, its tannin softened.

In good years that are not declared, houses may bottle a single quinta vintage, such as Taylor's Quinta de Vargellas. Our list has declared vintages back to 1977: Dow's and Graham's 2000, Graham's 1983, Niepoort 1987 and Taylor 1977.

card.front: Why must a Vintage Port be decanted?
card.back: It is bottled young and unfiltered after about two years in cask, so it throws a heavy crust of sediment as it ages in bottle.

items: Taylor Fladgate ‘Quinta de Vargellas’ Vintage Port 1987

components.name: Late Bottled Vintage Port
components.explain:
Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, is Port from a single year, like Vintage Port, but left in wood much longer, four to six years, before bottling. The longer cask time softens it and makes it ready to drink sooner.

Most LBV is filtered and ready on release; traditional unfiltered LBV keeps ageing and may throw a little sediment. It gives much of Vintage Port's dark fruit at a gentler price.

Ours are unusual: Feist's 2006 and Sandeman's 1999 have had long bottle age on top of their years in wood, so they are mature and mellow: dark cherry, plum, fig, cocoa and spice. Check for sediment and decant if any.

card.front: How is a Late Bottled Vintage different from Vintage Port?
card.back: Both are one year, but LBV stays four to six years in wood before bottling, so it softens sooner. Ours, Feist 2006 and Sandeman 1999, are mature.

components.name: Tawny and Colheita Port
components.explain:
Tawny Port ages for years in small, old casks, where slow contact with air turns its colour from ruby to amber and its fruit to walnut, caramel, dried orange peel and coffee. Most tawnies are blends, sold as 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old.

A Colheita is a tawny from a single harvest, colheita in Portuguese, aged at least seven years in cask and often far longer, with the harvest year and the bottling date on the label. Because it has aged with air in cask, it needs no decanting and keeps for weeks once opened.

Niepoort, a family house of Dutch origin, is famous for its Colheitas. Ours is the 1997 in a half-bottle. Serve it slightly cool with pecan desserts and the Bread Pudding.

card.front: What is a Colheita Port?
card.back: A tawny from one harvest, aged at least seven years in cask: walnut, caramel and orange peel. Ours is Niepoort 1997, no decanting needed.

components.name: Ageing under flor
components.explain:
Flor is a living layer of yeast that grows like a pale film on the surface of certain wines left in barrels that are not quite full. It shields the wine from air and feeds on it, giving a sharp, nutty, salty tang: green apple, almond, bread dough.

In southern Spain this is how fino and Manzanilla sherry are made; Sanlúcar's sea air keeps the flor thickest, which is why Manzanilla is so light and salty. In the Jura the same thing happens to Savagnin in barrels never topped up, for more than six years, making Vin Jaune: walnut, curry spice and dried apple.

Our La Cigarrera Manzanilla and the Pélican Vin Jaune are cousins under the skin. Both are bone dry and love salty food and cheese.

card.front: What do Manzanilla and Vin Jaune have in common?
card.back: Both age under flor, a film of yeast on the wine in part-filled barrels, giving a dry, nutty, salty tang. Ours: La Cigarrera and Pélican.

components.name: The solera
components.explain:
The solera is sherry's system of fractional blending. Barrels are arranged in tiers, called criaderas, with the oldest wine in the bottom row, the solera itself.

Each time wine is drawn for bottling, only part of each bottom barrel is taken. It is refilled from the tier above, and that from the tier above it, and so on, with new wine entering at the top. The young wine takes on the character of the old, and the solera keeps the style steady for decades; some soleras were begun more than a century ago.

That is why most sherry, including our La Cigarrera Manzanilla, carries no vintage: every glass holds a little of every year.

card.front: Why does our Manzanilla carry no vintage?
card.back: It comes from a solera: tiers of barrels where each draw is topped up from younger tiers, so every glass blends many years and the style stays steady.

components.name: Estufagem and canteiro: heating Madeira
components.explain:
Madeira is the only wine deliberately cooked. After fortification it is heated, recreating the long tropical sea voyages that first made it famous.

Estufagem warms the wine in tanks to about 45 to 50 degrees Celsius for at least three months, a faster way for younger wines. Canteiro, the slow way for the finest, ages the wine in casks in the warm lofts of the lodge, under the roof, for years, sometimes decades.

The heat and air turn it amber and give coffee, caramel, toffee, dried fig and walnut, all held up by bright acidity. Our Broadbent Single Cask Malvasia 2009 is a single cask of one harvest, aged warm in old oak.

card.front: What are estufagem and canteiro?
card.back: Two ways to heat Madeira: estufagem warms it in tanks for months; canteiro ages it for years in casks in warm lofts, for the finest wines.

components.name: Old vines
components.explain:
Old vines, vieilles vignes in French, alte Reben in German, cepas vellas in Galician, is not a legal term anywhere, but it matters. As vines age, past thirty or forty years, they give fewer, smaller bunches, and their deep roots reach water and minerals far below the surface.

The wine tends to be more concentrated, textured and balanced, and less affected by drought or heavy rain. Some of our vines are very old indeed: Ridge's Lytton Springs has blocks planted in 1901, and Santorini's ungrafted vines are among the oldest anywhere.

On our list: Berres Old Vines, Châteaumar's fifty year old Syrah, Stein, Bründlmayer's Alte Reben, Do Ferreiro's Cepas Vellas, Saint Damien and Ridge. Say what the label claims, never an age you cannot confirm.

card.front: What do old vines give a wine?
card.back: Fewer, smaller bunches and deep roots: more concentration, texture and balance. Not a legal term, so quote only the age the label or sommelier confirms.

components.name: The field blend
components.explain:
A field blend is a vineyard planted with several grape varieties mixed together, row by row or vine by vine, then picked and fermented together. The blend is made in the vineyard, not in the cellar.

It was the old way in Europe and in early California, where Italian and other immigrant growers planted Zinfandel with Petite Sirah, Carignane, Grenache, Mataro and others for balance: one for colour, one for acidity, one for fruit.

Ridge's Lytton Springs, planted from 1901 and holding more than twenty varieties, is a textbook example, and Ridge's Three Valleys draws on old field grapes too. When a guest asks what is in it, the label lists the share of each grape.

card.front: What is a field blend?
card.back: Several grape varieties planted together and picked and fermented together, so the blend is made in the vineyard. Ridge's Lytton Springs is a classic.

components.name: Organic and biodynamic farming
components.explain:
Organic farming grows vines without synthetic herbicides, pesticides or fertilisers, using cover crops, compost and copper or sulphur sprays. Biodynamic farming goes further, following the ideas of Rudolf Steiner from the 1920s: it treats the vineyard as a living whole, uses herbal and mineral preparations and plans work by a lunar calendar.

Growers say it brings livelier soils and wines that show their place more clearly. Some are certified; others farm this way without a label.

Leflaive in Burgundy became a leader of biodynamic farming from 1997; Huet, Climens and d'Angerville farm biodynamically; Gouges, Saint Damien and Pépière organically; Châteaumar organically without certification. Describe the farming; never make a health claim for the wine.

card.front: What is the difference between organic and biodynamic farming?
card.back: Organic avoids synthetic sprays and fertilisers; biodynamic adds herbal preparations and a lunar calendar. Leflaive and Huet farm biodynamically. Never make a health claim.

components.name: Burgundy's four tiers
components.explain:
Burgundy ranks land, not producers. Every vineyard sits in one of four tiers, and the label tells you which.

At the base is the regional tier, Bourgogne, from anywhere in the region. Next come the village wines, named for a village such as Meursault or Nuits-Saint-Georges. Above them are Premier Cru vineyards, written 1er Cru, named after the village with the vineyard, such as Beaune Premier Cru Clos de la Mousse. At the top are the Grand Cru vineyards, so famous they carry only their own name, such as Echézeaux or Les Preuses in Chablis; they are a small share of all Burgundy.

So a label that names only a vineyard is usually the grandest. Our list climbs every rung, from the Damien Martin Bourgogne to Grivot's Echézeaux.

card.front: Name Burgundy's four tiers from bottom to top.
card.back: Regional (Bourgogne), village (such as Meursault), Premier Cru (village plus vineyard) and Grand Cru (the vineyard name alone, such as Echézeaux).

components.name: Grand Cru and Premier Cru in Champagne
components.explain:
In Champagne, cru means village rather than vineyard. Each of the region's villages was once rated on a scale, the échelle des crus, which set the price of its grapes. Seventeen villages, such as Bouzy, Aÿ, Cramant and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, are Grand Cru; about forty more, such as Vertus, are Premier Cru.

A Champagne may print Grand Cru or Premier Cru only if all its grapes come from villages of that rank. Most big-house blends draw on many villages and do not, though they use plenty of Grand Cru fruit.

On our list, Paul Bara and Pierre Paillard are Grand Cru from Bouzy; Larmandier-Bernier and Veuve Fourny are Premier Cru from Vertus; Pol Roger's Blanc de Blancs draws on the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs.

card.front: What does Grand Cru mean on a Champagne label?
card.back: Every grape came from one of the seventeen top-rated villages, such as Bouzy. In Champagne a cru is a village, not a single vineyard.

components.name: Clos and monopole
components.explain:
A clos is a vineyard enclosed by walls, many of them built by monks or nobles centuries ago in Burgundy and the Loire. The walls marked a prized piece of land and protected it.

A monopole is a vineyard owned entirely by one producer, rare in Burgundy, where most vineyards are split among many families. A clos can be a monopole, but not always.

Our walled vineyards include Bouchard's Clos de la Mousse in Beaune, a monopole since 1872; Roumier's Clos de la Bussière in Morey; d'Angerville's Clos des Ducs beside its house in Volnay; Lafon's Clos de la Baronne in Meursault; and Coudert's Clos de la Roilette in Fleurie. Say it simply: one family's walled vineyard.

card.front: What is a monopole in Burgundy?
card.back: A vineyard owned entirely by one producer, rare in Burgundy. Bouchard's Clos de la Mousse and d'Angerville's Clos des Ducs on our list are monopoles.

components.name: The 1855 classification
components.explain:
For the Paris Exposition of 1855, Emperor Napoleon III asked for a ranking of Bordeaux's best wines. The brokers ranked the red estates of the Médoc, plus Haut-Brion, into five growths, crus classés, by the prices their wines fetched, and the sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac into first and second growths, with Yquem alone above them as Premier Cru Supérieur.

It has barely changed since: Mouton Rothschild's promotion to first growth in 1973 was the one great change. Second wines and estates outside the list carry no rank.

On our list: Pichon Lalande, second growth; Talbot, fourth; Grand-Puy-Lacoste, fifth; Yquem, Premier Cru Supérieur; Climens and Suduiraut, first growths of Sauternes and Barsac.

card.front: What was the 1855 classification, and where does Yquem stand?
card.back: A ranking of Bordeaux estates by price for the Paris Exposition: Médoc reds in five growths, Sauternes in two, with Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur.

components.name: Second wines
components.explain:
Most great Bordeaux estates make a second wine. After the harvest the team tastes every lot, and only the best go into the grand vin, the château's main wine; younger vines and lots that do not quite make the cut go into the second wine.

A second wine comes from the same vineyards and cellar, is often softer and readier sooner, and costs much less. Famous examples include Les Forts de Latour and Carruades de Lafite.

Our La Chapelle de Meyney is the second wine of Château Meyney in Saint-Estèphe, from younger vines on the estate: blackcurrant, cedar and earth, a taste of the Médoc for a gentler price.

card.front: What is a second wine in Bordeaux?
card.back: Wine from the same estate and cellar that did not make the main blend, often younger vines: softer and kinder in price. Ours is La Chapelle de Meyney.

components.name: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva
components.explain:
Rioja labels promise how long a wine has aged before release. Crianza has at least two years, one of them in oak. Reserva has at least three, one in oak. Gran Reserva, made only in good years, has at least five, with at least two in oak and the rest in bottle.

Traditional houses go well beyond the minimums. The long ageing softens the tannin and turns the fruit savoury: dried cherry, strawberry, tobacco, leather, vanilla and sweet spice.

La Rioja Alta ages its Gran Reserva 904 about four years in American oak barrels from its own cooperage, then years in bottle before release. It is the bottle for a guest who loves mellow, old-style red with lamb or duck.

card.front: What does Gran Reserva on a Rioja guarantee?
card.back: At least five years of ageing, two in oak, from a good year. Our La Rioja Alta 904 spends about four years in American oak.

components.name: Smaragd and the Wachau categories
components.explain:
The Wachau's growers, through their association Vinea Wachau, sort their dry wines into three categories by ripeness and weight, each named after something of the valley.

Steinfeder, after a feathery grass of the terraces, is the lightest. Federspiel, after the lure falconers used, is the classic, medium-bodied style. Smaragd, the emerald lizard that suns itself on the stone walls, is the ripest and fullest, still dry, from the best sites.

Our Franz Hirtzberger Honivogl is a Grüner Veltliner Smaragd from Spitz: ripe pear, quince, white pepper and honeyed spice, rich and powerful yet dry. It stands up to roast meats as well as fish.

card.front: What is a Smaragd, and what is it named after?
card.back: The Wachau's ripest, fullest dry wine category, named for an emerald lizard on the terrace walls. Our Hirtzberger Honivogl is a Grüner Smaragd.

components.name: Opening sparkling wine
components.explain:
A bottle of Champagne holds about six atmospheres of pressure, roughly three times a car tyre, so it is opened with care, and quietly.

Chill it to 43 to 46°F. Present the label to the host. Loosen the cage but keep a thumb or a napkin over the cork from then on. Hold the bottle at about 45 degrees, pointed away from guests, grip the cork and turn the bottle, not the cork, easing it out so it leaves with a soft sigh rather than a pop.

Pour a little into each glass to let the foam settle, then top up to about two thirds, guests first and the host last. Return the bottle to the ice bucket, half ice and half water.

card.front: How do you open Champagne at the table?
card.back: Cage loosened, thumb on the cork, bottle at 45 degrees away from guests. Turn the bottle, not the cork, for a soft sigh, never a pop.

components.name: Sabrage
components.explain:
Sabrage is opening a bottle of Champagne with a sabre. Legend ties it to Napoleon's cavalry, the hussars, celebrating victories on horseback.

A well-chilled bottle is held at about 45 degrees, pointed into open space. The blunt back of an unsharpened Champagne sabre slides firmly up the seam of the bottle and strikes the lip; the pressure inside and the weak point where the seam meets the collar break the glass cleanly, and the collar flies off with the cork still in it.

The house sabres in the courtyard on Fridays at five; confirm on shift. Only those trained by the house perform it; a new server's role is to know the story and keep guests well clear, never to try it.

card.front: What is sabrage, and when does Brennan's do it?
card.back: Opening Champagne with a sabre struck up the seam to the lip, breaking off the collar with the cork. The house sabres in the courtyard on Fridays at five.

components.name: Coravin: the needle through the cork
components.explain:
The Coravin system lets us pour a glass of a fine still wine without pulling the cork. A thin, hollow needle passes through the cork; the bottle is pressurised with argon, an inert gas, which pushes the wine out through the needle. When the needle is withdrawn, the natural cork closes up again and the argon protects the wine left inside.

So a bottle such as the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé can be poured by the glass over weeks without spoiling, and a guest can taste a great white Burgundy without buying the bottle.

At the table, say: poured by Coravin, so the bottle is never opened. Present the label. Who handles the device and the house's limits are questions for the bar.

card.front: How does Coravin pour the Leflaive without opening it?
card.back: A hollow needle goes through the cork, argon gas pushes the wine out, and the cork reseals, so the rest stays fresh for weeks.

components.name: Coravin Sparkling
components.explain:
A needle cannot help a sparkling wine, because the bottle must be opened to pour. Coravin Sparkling is a different device: a stopper that clamps onto an opened bottle and a charger that refills the space with gas, so the wine keeps its pressure and its bubbles.

It lets the Rare Champagne be poured by the glass at $75 from an opened bottle. The cork has been pulled, so do not say no cork is pulled; say poured by the glass from a bottle kept fresh under the Coravin Sparkling stopper, and reseal right after each pour.

The maker says a bottle stays fizzy for weeks; how long the house keeps an opened bottle in service is a question for the bar, as is reading the vintage, 2012 or 2013, on the label.

card.front: How is the Rare Champagne kept fresh by the glass?
card.back: Under a Coravin Sparkling stopper that re-pressurises the opened bottle. The cork is out, so reseal right after each pour and confirm the house limit.

components.name: Decanting
components.explain:
Decanting means pouring a wine from its bottle into a carafe, for one of two reasons.

An old red or a Vintage Port throws sediment. Stand the bottle upright for some hours if possible, open it gently, and pour slowly in one steady motion over a light or candle, stopping when the sediment reaches the neck. A young, powerful red, such as a Napa Cabernet or a Châteauneuf, is decanted for air, which softens tannin and opens the aroma; thirty to forty-five minutes helps.

Very old wines can fade quickly once decanted, so open them close to drinking. The sommelier decides which bottles need it; offer it, explain why, and always show the bottle and keep it beside the decanter.

card.front: Give the two reasons to decant a wine.
card.back: To leave sediment behind in an old red or Vintage Port, or to give a young, powerful red air. The sommelier decides; keep the bottle beside the decanter.

components.name: Half-bottle service
components.explain:
A half-bottle holds 375 ml, half a standard bottle: two or three glasses of table wine, or four or five small pours of a sweet wine. It is the server's best friend at a table of two, or for a table that wants a different wine with each course.

Wine ages faster in a half-bottle, because there is more air and glass for each drop of wine, so mature half-bottles can be at their peak sooner than the same wine in a full bottle.

Our half-bottle list is long and serious: Krug, Yquem, Meursault, Chablis, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Vintage Port. Present it like any bottle, pour smaller first glasses so everyone gets a second, and suggest one white and one red half for a long meal.

card.front: Why suggest half-bottles, and how many glasses do they pour?
card.back: Two or three glasses, or four or five small sweet pours: ideal for two, or a different wine each course, such as a white half then a red half.

components.name: Magnums and large formats
components.explain:
A magnum holds 1.5 litres, two standard bottles; a double magnum, called a Jeroboam in Champagne, holds 3 litres, four bottles. Larger bottles still have Biblical names, such as Rehoboam and Methuselah.

Wine ages more slowly and gracefully in large bottles, because there is less air for each drop of wine, which is why collectors prize them. And nothing makes a table's toast like a magnum.

Our large formats include the Billecart-Salmon 80th anniversary magnum, the Bollinger and Piper-Heidsieck magnums, the Taittinger double magnum and Prüm's Auslese in magnum. Carry it with both hands, open it like any Champagne, pour in small first pours, and keep it in a deep bucket.

card.front: How many standard bottles are in a magnum and a double magnum?
card.back: A magnum is 1.5 litres, two bottles; a double magnum is 3 litres, four. Wine ages more slowly in large bottles.

components.name: Serving sweet and fortified wine
components.explain:
Sweet wines are rich, so they are served in small pours, usually two to three ounces, in a smaller glass. A half-bottle pours four or five.

Serve sweet whites such as Sauternes, Auslese and icewine well chilled, about 45 to 50°F, so they taste fresh rather than syrupy. Serve Port, Madeira and Banyuls a little cooler than room temperature, about 60 to 64°F.

The golden rule of pairing: the wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert, or the dessert makes it taste thin and sour. Offer a sweet wine when the dessert menu arrives, not after. Fortified wines keep for days or weeks once opened; Madeira and tawny Port keep longest.

card.front: What is the golden rule for pairing wine with dessert?
card.back: The wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it tastes thin and sour. Serve small pours, sweet whites well chilled.

components.name: Serving a mature bottle
components.explain:
A mature wine has spent years, sometimes decades, ageing in bottle. Its fruit turns from fresh to dried, its tannin softens, and new notes appear: leather, forest floor and mushroom in reds; honey, nuts and petrol in Riesling; caramel and coffee in Port.

Mature bottles need gentle handling. Carry them as they lay, without shaking; stand older reds and Ports upright ahead of time if you can; open slowly, as old corks crumble, and keep a two-pronged cork puller or a decanter ready. Taste for soundness with the sommelier before pouring for the table.

Our list is rich in age: Pichon Lalande 2004, Beaucastel 2007, Gilette 1989, Riveyrac 1975, Taylor 1977 and more. Tell guests the age is the point: they are drinking time.

card.front: How do you handle an old bottle before serving?
card.back: Carry it gently as it lay, stand reds and Port upright ahead, open slowly as old corks crumble, and check soundness with the sommelier first.

components.name: Presenting and pouring a bottle
components.explain:

components.name: A corked bottle
components.explain:
A corked wine has been tainted by a compound called TCA, usually from the cork. It smells of wet cardboard, a damp cellar or a musty basement, and the fruit seems flat and muted. It affects a small share of bottles sealed with natural cork, and it is never anyone's fault at the table.

When the host tastes and frowns, smell the cork and the glass, or ask the sommelier to. If the wine is faulty, apologise, take the bottle away and bring another, without debate.

Other faults are rarer: a bottle that is oxidised, flat and brown, or cooked by heat. A wine the guest simply dislikes is a different matter, for the sommelier or manager to handle.

card.front: What does a corked wine smell like, and what do you do?
card.back: Wet cardboard or a damp cellar, the fruit muted. Apologise, remove it and bring another without debate; it is the cork's fault, not the guest's.

components.name: The Grand Award cellar
components.explain:
Brennan's wine cellar is one of the few in the world to hold Wine Spectator's Grand Award, the magazine's highest honour, given for depth, breadth, mature vintages and harmony with the menu. The house's own notes say it first won the award in 1983.

Then came Hurricane Katrina in 2005. A month without power cooked the cellar, and about 35,000 bottles were lost. After the restaurant reopened, the team rebuilt the collection, and the house notes say it won the Grand Award back in 2021; reports of the 2025 awards name it again, with about 3,000 to 3,600 selections, deepest in Burgundy, Champagne, Bordeaux and California.

Every bottle you present comes from that rebuilt cellar. Confirm the award years from the listing at lineup before quoting them.

card.front: What happened to the Brennan's cellar, and what has it won?
card.back: Katrina's power loss in 2005 cooked about 35,000 bottles. The rebuilt cellar holds Wine Spectator's Grand Award; confirm the years at lineup.

components.explain:
Champagne is woven into the house. Bubbles at Brennan's runs in the Roost Bar and Courtyard on weekday afternoons, with a list of sparkling rosé bottles from the Mirabelle to the Pommery, bubbly cocktails and bar snacks, and Champagne sabering on Fridays at five.

Birthday Bubbles is the page of Champagnes for celebrations: half-bottles of Drappier, Paul Bara and Krug for two, and magnums and a double magnum, Billecart-Salmon's 80th anniversary Sous Bois, Bollinger, Piper-Heidsieck and Taittinger, for a table.

Know which bottles are Champagne and which are sparkling wine from elsewhere: on the rosé list the Mirabelle and Louis Pommery are Californian. Confirm the hours and the sabering on shift.

components.name: Piper-Heidsieck and the house Champagne
components.explain:
Piper-Heidsieck was founded in Reims in 1785 by Florens-Louis Heidsieck, a cloth merchant from Westphalia who set out to make a cuvée worthy of a queen and presented his wine to Marie Antoinette. After his death his nephew's partner, Henri-Guillaume Piper, joined the business, and the two names were joined.

Today Piper-Heidsieck makes our house Champagne, an Extra Brut of Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay bottled under the Brennan's name, poured by the glass and by the bottle, and its Cuvée Brut in magnum on Birthday Bubbles.

Say labelled for us, not made for us; Piper-Heidsieck spells its own cuvée Essentiel, and which cuvée is in the bottle, and its dosage, is for the sommelier to confirm.

card.front: Who makes our house Champagne, and what is the house's royal story?
card.back: Piper-Heidsieck of Reims, founded in 1785 by Florens-Louis Heidsieck, who presented his wine to Marie Antoinette. Say labelled for us, not made for us.

components.name: Rare Champagne
components.explain:
Rare began as Piper-Heidsieck's prestige cuvée, first made from the 1976 harvest, a year of record heat. It is declared only in exceptional years, about a dozen vintages in half a century, and is now run as its own house, Rare Champagne, in Reims.

Its bottle wears a jewelled dress that recalls a design Fabergé made for the house in the nineteenth century. The wine is Chardonnay-led with Pinot Noir from Grand Cru sites, aged about a decade on its lees: white peach, candied citrus and toasted almond.

We pour Rare 2012 by the glass under the Coravin Sparkling stopper and list the 2013 by the bottle; the glass page now prints a 2013, so read the label before naming the vintage.

card.front: When was Rare first made, and how is it poured by the glass?
card.back: From the 1976 harvest, as Piper-Heidsieck's prestige cuvée, declared only in great years. We pour it under a Coravin Sparkling stopper.

components.name: Pommery, Charles Lafitte and Madame Pommery's brut
components.explain:
Pommery is a Reims house that dates itself to 1858, with roots in an earlier wine business of 1836. Its great figure was Madame Louise Pommery, a widow who took over the business and, in 1874, launched Pommery Nature, the first brut Champagne to succeed commercially, at a time when most Champagne was very sweet. The British loved it, and dry Champagne became the world's taste.

Pommery now belongs to the Vranken-Pommery group, which also owns Charles Lafitte, a name with roots to 1834 in Épernay, and makes the Louis Pommery sparkling rosé in California.

So three bottles on our lists share one family: the Charles Lafitte on both tastings, the Pommery rosé and the Louis Pommery rosé, and only the first two are Champagne.

card.front: What did Madame Pommery give the world in 1874?
card.back: Pommery Nature, the first commercially successful brut, dry Champagne. Pommery's group also makes our Charles Lafitte and the California Louis Pommery.

components.name: Krug and the Grande Cuvée
components.explain:
Krug was founded in Reims in 1843 by Joseph Krug, who believed a house's finest Champagne should be its blend rather than a single vintage. That idea still drives it.

Each year Krug builds its Grande Cuvée from more than a hundred wines from ten or more harvests, fermented in small old oak casks, then ages it for years more. Each release is a numbered edition, counted from the founder's first blend, and a Krug ID code on the back label tells which harvest it is built on.

Our menu prints it as Grand Cuvée; Krug spells it Grande Cuvée. We pour it in a half-bottle on Birthday Bubbles, and which edition is inside is a question for the sommelier.

card.front: What makes Krug Grande Cuvée different from other non-vintage Champagne?
card.back: It blends more than a hundred wines from ten or more years, aged long, and each release is a numbered edition. Founded in Reims in 1843.

components.name: Billecart-Salmon and our 80th anniversary magnum
components.explain:
Billecart-Salmon was founded at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ in 1818, on the marriage of Nicolas François Billecart and Elisabeth Salmon, and it is still family owned, now in its seventh generation. It is famous for finesse and for its rosé.

Its prestige rosé is named for Elisabeth Salmon, whose marriage gave the house its name: our Cuvée Elisabeth Salmon Rosé 2009 is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with long age before release.

For Brennan's eightieth year the house has a Billecart-Salmon Sous Bois magnum labelled for the anniversary, its base wines fermented in oak. It is the Birthday Bubbles bottle with a story the guest can take home: the restaurant began in 1946. Confirm the anniversary bottling with the sommelier.

card.front: What is special about our Billecart-Salmon magnum?
card.back: It is the Sous Bois, oak-fermented, labelled for Brennan's 80th anniversary. Billecart-Salmon was founded in 1818 on the marriage that gave it its name.

components.name: Bollinger and James Bond
components.explain:
Bollinger is a family-owned house in Aÿ, the Grand Cru village famous for Pinot Noir, and its style is rich and powerful: Pinot Noir-led, part fermented in old oak, built on reserve wines kept in magnum.

It is also James Bond's Champagne. Bollinger appears in the Bond novels and, from Live and Let Die in 1973, in almost every Bond film since. That film was shot partly in New Orleans; its famous jazz funeral scene was filmed in the French Quarter at the corner of Chartres and Dumaine, a few blocks from Royal Street.

We pour the Special Cuvée by the bottle and in magnum, and the PNTX20, an all-Pinot Noir edition led by the village of Tauxières.

card.front: What links Bollinger, James Bond and New Orleans?
card.back: Bond drinks Bollinger on screen from Live and Let Die (1973), a film shot partly in the French Quarter. Bollinger is a family house in Aÿ.

components.name: Taittinger
components.explain:
Taittinger is one of the few great Champagne houses still run by its family. Pierre Taittinger bought the old Reims house of Forest-Fourneaux, founded in 1734, in the early 1930s and gave it his name; the house later made its home in the thirteenth century buildings of the Counts of Champagne in Reims, the source of its prestige Comtes de Champagne.

Its style leans on Chardonnay, unusually generous in its house Brut, which gives elegance and freshness.

On our lists: La Française, its house Brut, in a double magnum on Birthday Bubbles, the same Champagne that tops the Flamingo in the Roost; and the Prestige Rosé on the Bubbles rosé page.

card.front: What gives Taittinger its elegance, and where else do guests meet it?
card.back: A generous share of Chardonnay. La Française, its Brut, is in our double magnum and tops the Flamingo cocktail in the Roost.

components.name: Moët & Chandon and Napoleon
components.explain:
Moët & Chandon was founded in Épernay in 1743 by Claude Moët and is now one of the largest Champagne producers in the world. His grandson Jean-Rémy Moët was a friend of Napoleon Bonaparte, who visited the house several times; the Impérial name pays homage to the emperor.

Moët is pronounced moh-ET, sounding the t, a name of Dutch origin.

We pour two pinks: the Imperial Rosé on the Bubbles list, a dry Brut rosé Champagne, Pinot Noir-led and coloured with red wine, and the Nectar Impérial Rosé on the bottle list, a Demi-Sec, noticeably sweet, for desserts. Never confuse the two at the table.

card.front: Which Moët rosé is dry and which is sweet?
card.back: The Imperial Rosé is dry, a Brut; the Nectar Impérial Rosé is Demi-Sec, sweet, for dessert. Moët is pronounced moh-ET, founded in Épernay in 1743.

components.name: Pol Roger and Winston Churchill
components.explain:
Pol Roger is a family Champagne house in Épernay, and its most famous customer was Winston Churchill. He drank it from 1908 and befriended Odette Pol-Roger at the British Embassy in Paris in 1944; she sent him a case every birthday.

When Churchill died in 1965, the house put a black border around the labels of the bottles it shipped to Britain in mourning, and its prestige Cuvée Sir Winston Churchill was created from the 1975 vintage.

Our bottle is its vintage Blanc de Blancs 2015, all Chardonnay from the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs: lemon, white flowers and chalk. A guest who loves history will love the story.

card.front: Whose Champagne was Pol Roger, and how did the house mourn him?
card.back: Winston Churchill's. After his death in 1965 the house put a black border on its labels shipped to Britain. We pour its Blanc de Blancs 2015.

components.name: Drappier and Charles de Gaulle
components.explain:
The Drappier family settled at Urville, in the Côte des Bar in Champagne's far south, in 1808, and still runs its house there.

Their most famous customer lived just down the road. General Charles de Gaulle's family home, La Boisserie, was at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, near Urville, and from 1965 he chose Drappier for his private receptions there. The house still makes a Cuvée Charles de Gaulle in his honour.

Our Drappier is the Carte d'Or Brut in a half-bottle on Birthday Bubbles, about three parts Pinot Noir with Chardonnay and Meunier: crisp, with citrus, orchard fruit and a toasty edge.

card.front: Which French president drank Drappier, and why?
card.back: Charles de Gaulle, whose home at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises was near Drappier's village of Urville. He chose it for his private receptions.

components.name: Laurent-Perrier
components.explain:
Laurent-Perrier was founded at Tours-sur-Marne in 1812. Its name joins two people: Eugène Laurent, a cellar master who took over the house, and his widow, Mathilde Emilie Perrier, who ran it after his death and added her name.

In 1939 it was bought by Marie-Louise de Nonancourt, and her son Bernard de Nonancourt led it for more than fifty years, making it one of the best-selling Champagne houses in the world while keeping it family led and independent. He was a pioneer of rosé Champagne made by skin contact.

Our bottle is the Harmony Demi-Sec in a half-bottle, gently sweet with pear, apricot and honey: a Champagne for dessert.

card.front: Whose two names make Laurent-Perrier?
card.back: Cellar master Eugène Laurent and his widow Mathilde Emilie Perrier, who ran the house after him. Our Harmony is a sweet Demi-Sec.

components.name: Houses, growers and cooperatives
components.explain:
Champagne is made by three kinds of producer. The great houses, such as Bollinger, Krug and Moët, buy most of their grapes from thousands of growers across the region and blend for a consistent house style. Cooperatives pool their members' grapes; Nicolas Feuillatte, based at Chouilly near Épernay, is the brand of a large growers' cooperative.

Grower Champagne is made by a family from its own vineyards, often in one village, and shows that place: look for RM, récoltant-manipulant, in small print on the label.

Our growers include Paul Bara and Pierre Paillard of Bouzy, Chartogne-Taillet of Merfy, and Larmandier-Bernier and Veuve Fourny of Vertus. Say: one family, its own vines, one village's voice.

card.front: What is grower Champagne, and how is it marked on a label?
card.back: Made by a family from its own vineyards, often one village: RM, récoltant-manipulant. Ours include Paul Bara, Pierre Paillard and Larmandier-Bernier.

components.name: Schramsberg and the Toast to Peace
components.explain:
Schramsberg is an old Calistoga estate at the north end of the Napa Valley, with caves dug into the hillside. Jack and Jamie Davies bought it in 1965 to make sparkling wine by the traditional method, and their first wine was a Blanc de Blancs, described as America's first commercial Chardonnay-based brut sparkling wine.

In February 1972, President Richard Nixon served the Schramsberg Blanc de Blancs 1969 at the Toast to Peace in Beijing with Premier Zhou Enlai, the first American wine poured at such a state event, and Schramsberg says its wines have been served by every administration since.

We pour its Blanc de Blancs half-bottle and the Mirabelle Brut Rosé, its North Coast label. Both are sparkling wine, not Champagne.

card.front: Which of our sparkling wines was poured at the Toast to Peace in 1972?
card.back: Schramsberg Blanc de Blancs, served by President Nixon in Beijing. We pour its Blanc de Blancs and its Mirabelle rosé.

components.name: Argyle
components.explain:
Argyle opened in 1987 in Dundee, in Oregon's Willamette Valley, working out of a former nut processing plant, and sparkling wine was its signature from the very first year. Its founders believed the valley's cool climate was ideal for the traditional method.

Today it farms vineyards in the Dundee Hills and the Eola-Amity Hills and makes Pinot Noir and Chardonnay as well as sparkling wine.

Our glass is the Argyle 2022, printed as Vintage Brut on the glass list and as Brut elsewhere: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with a little Meunier, shortbread, apple and citrus zest with a saline finish. It is not Champagne: say American sparkling wine, and confirm the blend with the sommelier.

card.front: What is Argyle, and what must you never call it?
card.back: A Willamette Valley winery, founded in 1987, with sparkling wine its signature. It is American sparkling wine, never Champagne. We pour the 2022 by the glass.

components.name: Ridgeview and Chapel Down
components.explain:
England's sparkling wine pioneers planted on the same chalk that runs under Champagne. Ridgeview was founded in the mid 1990s near the village of Ditchling, on the South Downs in Sussex, as a family estate devoted to sparkling wine. Its Grosvenor Blanc de Blancs famously won a major international sparkling wine trophy, the first non-Champagne to do so.

Chapel Down, at Tenterden in Kent, grew into England's largest wine producer. Its vineyards face south on chalk and its wines are made by the traditional method.

We pour Ridgeview's Bloomsbury, Chardonnay-led, and Chapel Down's Rosé Brut. Say English sparkling wine with pride: it is a real category now, not a novelty.

card.front: Where do Ridgeview and Chapel Down come from?
card.back: Ridgeview from Ditchling on the Sussex South Downs; Chapel Down from Tenterden in Kent, England's largest producer. Both on Champagne's chalk seam.

components.name: Domaine Leflaive
components.explain:
Domaine Leflaive is the most famous estate of Puligny-Montrachet, a family name synonymous with great white Burgundy. The family's roots in the village go back to 1717, but the modern domaine was built from about 1920 by Joseph Leflaive, an engineer who replanted and began selling under his own name.

His granddaughter Anne-Claude Leflaive ran it from 1990 until her death in 2015 and converted the whole domaine to biodynamic farming in 1997, a lead the rest of Burgundy followed. The domaine also farms vines at Verzé in the Mâconnais.

On our list: the Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin by the glass and by the bottle, a village Puligny 2016 and the Sous le Dos d'Ane Meursault Premier Cru 2017.

card.front: What is Domaine Leflaive famous for, and what do we pour by the glass?
card.back: Great white Burgundy from Puligny-Montrachet and a biodynamic lead from 1997. We pour its Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin, by the glass.

items: Domaine Leflaive ‘Sous le Dos d’Ane’ Meursault Premier Cru 2017

components.name: The Lafon family of Meursault
components.explain:
Domaine des Comtes Lafon is one of the great estates of Meursault. Comte Jules Lafon built it after his marriage in 1894, buying plots in the best vineyards of Meursault and Volnay and a piece of Le Montrachet.

As mayor of Meursault, in 1923 he invited friends to a harvest banquet that became the Paulée de Meursault, now the last of Burgundy's three great November feasts, the Trois Glorieuses, where growers bring their best bottles to share.

The family's Clos de la Baronne is a walled vineyard it owns entirely, and its Mâconnais estate, Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon, makes our Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine: the Lafon touch at a gentler price.

card.front: Which Burgundy feast did Comte Jules Lafon begin?
card.back: The Paulée de Meursault, a harvest banquet he gave as mayor in 1923. We pour Lafon's Clos de la Baronne Meursault and its Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine.
