Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine 2023

components.name: Maison Louis Jadot
components.explain:
Louis Jadot is one of the great houses of Beaune. The Jadot family came from Belgium and bought its first vineyard, the Clos des Ursules in Beaune, in 1826; Louis Henry Denis Jadot founded the house in 1859.

Like most Burgundy houses it both owns vineyards and buys grapes from growers, and makes wine from Chablis to Beaujolais. The head of Bacchus, god of wine, on every label is its emblem.

Three of our wines carry the Bacchus head: the Beaune Premier Cru on the dinner tasting with the Redfish Véronique, and half-bottles of village Meursault and Beaujolais-Villages. Say: one of Burgundy's great family houses, from the wine capital, Beaune.

card.front: What emblem is on every Louis Jadot label?
card.back: The head of Bacchus. Jadot is a great Beaune house founded in 1859; its Beaune Premier Cru pours on our dinner tasting.

components.name: Bouchard Père & Fils and the Clos de la Mousse
components.explain:
Bouchard Père & Fils was founded in Beaune in 1731, one of the oldest houses in Burgundy. Its wines age in the deep cellars of the Château de Beaune, a fifteenth century royal fortress the house has occupied since 1820, and it is one of the largest owners of Premier and Grand Cru vineyards on the Côte d'Or.

The Clos de la Mousse is a small walled Premier Cru of Beaune, about three and a half hectares, that Bouchard has owned outright since 1872: a monopole, so every bottle of it is Bouchard's.

Ours is the 2022 in a half-bottle: red cherry, raspberry, violet and a little spice, silky and fresh.

card.front: Why is every bottle of Clos de la Mousse made by Bouchard?
card.back: It is a monopole: a walled Beaune Premier Cru that Bouchard has owned alone since 1872. The house, founded in 1731, ages wine in the Château de Beaune.

components.name: Château London and the two Fichets
components.explain:
Two different Fichets are on our lists, and servers mix them up.

The dinner tasting's white, Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé, comes from Domaine Fichet of Igé in the Mâconnais, a family estate farmed by the Fichet brothers. Château London is a named vineyard parcel at Igé, old limestone with some vines over a century old. There is no castle and it has nothing to do with England. It is made mostly in steel with a touch of old oak.

Jean-Philippe Fichet is a separate grower in Meursault, in the Côte de Beaune, known for precise white Burgundy; his Bourgogne Blanc is on the bottle list.

So say Fichet of Igé for the tasting, Jean-Philippe Fichet of Meursault for the bottle.

card.front: Is Château London a castle in England?
card.back: Neither: it is a vineyard parcel at Igé in the Mâconnais, farmed by Domaine Fichet of Igé. Jean-Philippe Fichet of Meursault is a different grower.

components.name: Damien Martin of Davayé
components.explain:
Our red Burgundy by the glass comes from a father and son domaine in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy: Domaine Robert et Damien Martin at Davayé, near Pouilly-Fuissé. Robert Martin founded it in 1982, and his son Damien now runs its roughly twenty hectares.

The Mâconnais is white wine country, so their Bourgogne Pinot Noir is a family's red made for drinking: red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, light in tannin and fresh.

It is the easiest red on the list for fish, crab and the lighter dishes, and the gentlest introduction to red Burgundy for a guest who usually orders Cabernet.

card.front: Who makes our Bourgogne Pinot Noir by the glass?
card.back: Domaine Robert et Damien Martin, a father and son domaine at Davayé in the Mâconnais, founded in 1982: light, red cherry Pinot Noir.

components.name: The family growers of the Côte de Beaune
components.explain:
Most of Burgundy is farmed by families with a few hectares spread over several villages, and many of our white Burgundies come from such domaines.

Thierry and Pascale Matrot run a family domaine in Meursault. Domaine Dupont-Fahn, in Tailly just south of Meursault, farms Les Tillets, one of the village's highest vineyards. Bitouzet-Prieur has vines in Meursault's Les Corbins. Paul Pillot is a Chassagne-Montrachet family that makes our Saint-Aubin Le Charmois. François Carillon comes from a family that has farmed Puligny for centuries and set up his own domaine in 2010. Tollot-Beaut, in Chorey-lès-Beaune, makes our Savigny Les Lavières.

Say the family name and the village: in Burgundy that is the whole story.

card.front: Name three family growers behind our white Burgundies.
card.back: Matrot and Dupont-Fahn of Meursault, Paul Pillot of Chassagne, and François Carillon of Puligny, whose family has farmed there for centuries.

items: Thierry et Pascale Matrot Bourgogne Blanc 2022 (375 ml)
Domaine Paul Pillot ‘Le Charmois’ Saint-Aubin Premier Cru 2022
Domaine Tollot-Beaut ‘Les Lavières’ Savigny-lès-Beaune Premier Cru 2019

components.name: Dauvissat and Louis Michel of Chablis
components.explain:
Two families on our list show the two faces of Chablis.

Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat is one of the two great reference estates of Chablis, a family domaine that ages its wines partly in old oak barrels, which adds texture without the taste of wood. Its Les Preuses Grand Cru 2015 now has years in bottle: lemon peel, oyster shell and a little honey, steely and deep.

Domaine Louis Michel takes the other path: every wine, even its Premier and Grand Crus, is made in steel tanks with no oak at all, for the purest expression of Chablis. We pour its village Chablis and its Montmains Premier Cru half-bottle.

Old oak or none: both are Chablis at its finest.

card.front: How do Dauvissat and Louis Michel differ in the cellar?
card.back: Dauvissat ages part of its Chablis in old oak for texture; Louis Michel makes every wine in steel with no oak at all.

items: Domaine Louis Michel ‘Montmains’ Chablis Premier Cru 2023 (375 ml)
Domaine René et Vincent Dauvissat ‘Les Preuses’ Chablis Grand Cru 2015

components.name: The great families of the Côte de Nuits
components.explain:
Our red Burgundy pages are full of the Côte de Nuits' most respected families.

Domaine Henri Gouges, farmed organically and run by its fourth generation, is the reference name of Nuits-Saint-Georges. Domaine Jean Grivot is a family domaine of Vosne-Romanée, run today by the next generation of the family, making our Echézeaux Grand Cru and Nuits Les Charmois. Domaine Georges Roumier of Chambolle-Musigny is one of Burgundy's most sought-after growers, and owns the walled Clos de la Bussière in Morey-Saint-Denis outright. Faiveley, a family house based in Nuits-Saint-Georges, makes our Bourgogne Rouge.

These are bottles for guests who know Burgundy. Speak the family name with respect, and let the sommelier lead on the oldest.

card.front: Which family is the reference name of Nuits-Saint-Georges?
card.back: Domaine Henri Gouges, farmed organically, fourth generation. Grivot of Vosne-Romanée and Roumier of Chambolle-Musigny are also on our red Burgundy list.

items: Domaine Henri Gouges ‘Les Pruliers’ Nuits-Saint-Georges Premier Cru 2016
Domaine Georges Roumier ‘Clos de la Bussière’ Morey-Saint-Denis Premier Cru 2014
Domaine Jean Grivot Echézeaux Grand Cru 2011

components.name: D'Angerville of Volnay and Domaine du Pélican
components.explain:
Domaine Marquis d'Angerville is a family domaine in Volnay, farmed biodynamically and known for perfumed, silky Pinot Noir. Its Clos des Ducs is the walled Premier Cru beside the family house, a monopole: no one else makes it.

The same family looked beyond Burgundy to the Jura, where it founded Domaine du Pélican at Arbois, bringing Burgundian care to the Jura's own grapes and its traditions, including Vin Jaune.

So two very different bottles on our list share one family: the Clos des Ducs Volnay Premier Cru 2014, red cherry, rose and violet, and the Pélican Vin Jaune 2016, walnut and curry spice. A lovely link to share with a guest who orders either.

card.front: What links our Volnay Clos des Ducs and the Pélican Vin Jaune?
card.back: One family: d'Angerville of Volnay, which owns the walled Clos des Ducs and founded Domaine du Pélican in the Jura.

items: Marquis d’Angerville ‘Clos des Ducs’ Volnay Premier Cru 2014
Domaine du Pélican Vin Jaune Arbois 2016

components.name: Côte d'Or names in the Mâconnais
components.explain:
The Mâconnais was long seen as Burgundy's humble south. Over the past decades famous families from further north have invested there, drawn by old vines, limestone and fair prices.

Domaine Leflaive of Puligny farms vines at Verzé; the Lafon family of Meursault formed Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon around Milly-Lamartine; and Domaine du Roc des Boutires in Pouilly-Fuissé has been owned since 2016 by the Parinet family of Château du Moulin-à-Vent, whose En Bertilionne is a small east-facing parcel below the Roche de Solutré.

That is why our Mâcon whites taste finer than their prices suggest. Say: a great Côte d'Or name, from the sunnier south.

card.front: Why do our Mâcon whites carry such famous names?
card.back: Côte d'Or families have invested in the Mâconnais: Leflaive at Verzé, Lafon at Milly-Lamartine, and the Parinet family at Roc des Boutires.

items: Domaine du Roc des Boutires ‘En Bertilionne’ Pouilly-Fuissé 2020
Les Héritiers du Comte Lafon Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine 2023

components.name: Lapierre, Foillard and the Beaujolais revival
components.explain:
By the 1970s much Beaujolais was industrial, sugared and fermented with cultured yeast. A small band of growers in the village of Villié-Morgon set out to change that, inspired by the oenologist Jules Chauvet: Marcel Lapierre, Jean Foillard, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton, nicknamed the Gang of Four by their American importer.

They went back to old vines, late picking, whole bunches, native yeasts and little or no added sulphur, and their silky, vivid Morgon wines became a root of the natural wine movement. Lapierre's children run his estate now.

We pour the Lapierre Morgon and Foillard's Côte du Py. Coudert's walled Clos de la Roilette in Fleurie is a family estate in the same spirit of fine, honest Gamay.

card.front: Who were the Gang of Four of Beaujolais?
card.back: Marcel Lapierre, Jean Foillard, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton of Morgon, who revived whole-bunch, native-yeast Gamay. We pour Lapierre and Foillard.

items: Domaine Coudert ‘Clos de la Roilette’ Fleurie 2023

components.name: Domaine Huet of Vouvray
components.explain:
Domaine Huet is the great estate of Vouvray. Victor Huet, a veteran of the First World War who had run a bistro in Paris, founded it in 1928 with his son Gaston, who ran it for decades until his death in 2002.

It farms three famous vineyards: Le Haut-Lieu, where it began; the Clos du Bourg, bought in 1953; and Le Mont, bought in 1957. All are Chenin Blanc, farmed biodynamically, and each is made sec, demi-sec or moelleux as the year allows.

We pour Le Haut-Lieu Sec in two vintages, Le Mont Demi-Sec and Le Mont Moelleux 2009. Teach the guest the three words, and let the vineyard name lead.

card.front: When was Domaine Huet founded, and what are its three vineyards?
card.back: In 1928 by Victor and Gaston Huet. Le Haut-Lieu, the Clos du Bourg and Le Mont, all Chenin Blanc, farmed biodynamically.

items: Domaine Huet ‘Le Haut-Lieu’ Vouvray Sec 2019 (375 ml)
Domaine Huet ‘Le Mont’ Vouvray Demi-Sec 2023 (375 ml)

components.name: Pascal Cotat of Chavignol
components.explain:
The Cotat family of Chavignol is one of Sancerre's most famous names among sommeliers. Pascal Cotat farms a few hectares on the village's steepest chalk slopes, including Les Monts Damnés, worked by hand.

His Sauvignon Blanc is picked riper than most Sancerre and made simply in old casks, so it is rich yet taut, and it ages for years in a way Sancerre rarely does. His rosé, Pinot Noir from a tiny parcel the family has farmed for decades, is bottled by lot rather than vintage, which is why our label reads Lot 2024.

Both are small and sought after. Present them as cult bottles of the Loire.

card.front: Why does our Cotat rosé say Lot 2024 instead of a vintage?
card.back: Pascal Cotat bottles it by lot rather than vintage. His Sancerre from Les Monts Damnés is picked ripe and ages unusually well.

components.name: Pépière and Écu: Muscadet's new guard
components.explain:
For years Muscadet was sold as cheap seaside white. A handful of growers changed its reputation by farming carefully and leaving their best wines on the lees for years.

Marc Ollivier founded Domaine de la Pépière near Maisdon-sur-Sèvre in 1984 and farmed organically from the start, long before it was common. The domaine has vines in four of the new crus communaux, among them Monnières-Saint Fiacre, and its cru wines rest on their lees well beyond the seventeen months required.

Domaine de l'Écu, at Le Landreau, bottles its wines by the rock beneath the vines; Orthogneiss is named for an ancient rock.

Together they prove Muscadet can be serious and age.

card.front: How did growers like Pépière change Muscadet?
card.back: Careful, often organic farming and long ageing on the lees, bottled by cru or by rock, as at Pépière and Domaine de l'Écu.

items: Domaine de la Pépière ‘Monnières-Saint Fiacre’ Muscadet 2020

components.name: Laureau and Baumard of Anjou
components.explain:
Two Anjou families make our Chenin Blancs from either side of the Loire.

Damien Laureau is a grower in Savennières, the small appellation on the north bank famous for dry Chenin from schist. His L'Alliance is waxy and full, quince, beeswax and toasted nuts, with a firm, stony finish: a white for rich fish and poultry.

Domaine des Baumard is a family estate at Rochefort-sur-Loire, across the river. Its Clos Sainte Catherine is a walled vineyard in the Coteaux du Layon, made sweet; our 2006 is golden, with quince, honey, apricot and a little ginger.

Same grape, same few miles, opposite ends of the table.

card.front: Which Anjou Chenin is dry and which is sweet on our list?
card.back: Laureau's Savennières L'Alliance is dry and waxy; Baumard's Clos Sainte Catherine Coteaux du Layon 2006 is sweet and honeyed. Same grape, opposite ends.

items: Domaine des Baumard ‘Clos Sainte Catherine’ Coteaux du Layon 2006

components.name: Domaine du Pegau
components.explain:
Pegau is old Provençal for a wine jug, the kind found in the papal palace at Avignon. The Féraud family has farmed in Châteauneuf-du-Pape since the seventeenth century, and Paul Féraud and his daughter Laurence named the domaine Domaine du Pegau in 1987.

Its style is proudly traditional: mostly Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and other permitted grapes, fermented with whole bunches in cement and aged about two years in large old casks.

The Cuvée Réservée got its name because the family once sold most of its wine in bulk and reserved a small share to bottle themselves. Ours is the 2020: kirsch, plum, garrigue, leather and spice. Ring it in by bin, as the list carries several Pegau lines.

card.front: What does Pegau mean, and why Cuvée Réservée?
card.back: An old Provençal wine jug. The family once sold most wine in bulk and reserved a share to bottle themselves.

components.name: Château de Beaucastel
components.explain:
Château de Beaucastel has been run by the Perrin family since 1909. It is famous for growing all thirteen grape varieties permitted in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, red and white, and for giving Mourvèdre a far larger role than most neighbours, which makes its wine darker, more savoury and longer lived. It has farmed organically since about 1950.

The family also helped found Tablas Creek in California with an American importer, bringing Rhône grapes to Paso Robles.

Its Oenothèque bottles are older vintages held in the château's own cellar and released later, so they arrive in fine condition. Ours is the 2007: dried cherry, leather, truffle and garrigue, with silky tannin.

card.front: What is Château de Beaucastel famous for?
card.back: Growing all thirteen permitted Châteauneuf grapes and a large share of Mourvèdre. Its Oenothèque 2007 was held in the château's cellar before release.

components.name: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe
components.explain:
In 1898 Hippolyte Brunier planted vines on La Crau, a high plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape. In 1793 Claude Chappe had built one of his signal telegraph towers there, on the line that sent messages between Paris and Marseille, because it was one of the highest points around. The tower is long gone, but the name stayed.

La Crau is covered in large, round stones, galets roulés, that store the day's heat and give the wine warmth and depth. The Brunier family still runs the estate, and plays on the name: its younger wine is called Télégramme.

Ours is La Crau 2014: kirsch, dried cherry, garrigue, pepper and leather, warm and silky.

card.front: Why is it called Vieux Télégraphe?
card.back: Claude Chappe's signal telegraph tower stood on its La Crau plateau from 1793. The Brunier family planted there in 1898, among large round stones.

items: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe ‘La Crau’ Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2014

components.name: Saint Damien, Raspail-Ay and La Louisianne
components.explain:
Gigondas is a village of family estates, and our two are among them.

Domaine Saint-Damien has been farmed by the Saurel family since the early nineteenth century and is certified organic. Its La Louisianne comes from old vines on the middle terraces of Gigondas: Grenache with Mourvèdre, Cinsault and a little Syrah, co-fermented in concrete. The name, which guests from New Orleans will love, belongs to a lieu-dit, a named parcel; why the parcel carries it is a question for the sommelier, not a story to invent.

Domaine Raspail-Ay is a family estate under the Dentelles de Montmirail; ours is a half-bottle of its Gigondas, Grenache-led with Syrah.

card.front: Why is a Gigondas called La Louisianne?
card.back: It is the name of a lieu-dit, a named parcel, farmed by the Saurel family. Why the parcel bears it is for the sommelier; never invent a Louisiana link.

components.name: Durban and Châteaumar: the Rhône by the glass
components.explain:
Our two Rhône reds by the glass each come with a twist.

Domaine de Durban, high above Beaumes-de-Venise, is famous for its sweet Muscat; the wine we pour is its dry red, Grenache and Syrah: ripe dark cherry, plum, dried herbs and pepper.

Domaine de Châteaumar's Cuvée Vincent, the breakfast tasting's red with the petite filet, is all Syrah from fifty year old vines on two parcels beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, about nine kilometres from Orange, farmed organically without certification. All Syrah is unusual in the south, where Grenache usually leads.

So: the sweet-wine estate's dry red, and the Grenache country's Syrah.

card.front: What is the twist in our Durban and Châteaumar reds?
card.back: Durban is famous for sweet Muscat but we pour its dry red; Châteaumar is all Syrah, unusual in the Grenache-led south.

items: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône 2023

components.name: Domaine Tempier and the Peyraud family
components.explain:
In 1936 Lucien Peyraud and his wife Lucie Tempier, known to everyone as Lulu, took on her family's farm at Le Plan du Castellet, above the port of Bandol. Lucien fell for an old bottle of Bandol and worked to have it recognised as its own appellation, granted in 1941, and he championed Mourvèdre, the grape that defines it.

Lulu's Provençal cooking, generous and seasonal, inspired Alice Waters of Chez Panisse and a generation of American chefs; she died in 2020 aged 102. Their family still owns the domaine.

Our bottle is the Tempier Bandol Rosé, Mourvèdre-led: wild strawberry, blood orange, garrigue and a savoury depth. It is the rosé for a guest who cooks.

card.front: Who were Lucien and Lulu Peyraud?
card.back: The couple behind Domaine Tempier from 1936: Lucien helped found the Bandol appellation and championed Mourvèdre; Lulu's cooking inspired Alice Waters.

components.name: Domaine de Trévallon
components.explain:
Domaine de Trévallon is a family estate in the Alpilles hills of Provence, near Les Baux. Its founder planted vines on land cleared from rock and garrigue and chose the grapes he believed in, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah for the red, rather than the blend the local rules came to require.

So Trévallon left the appellation and labels its wines with the wider regional name, Alpilles, and they have become among the most sought-after wines in the south of France, proof that a great wine does not need an official name.

Its white is rare: Marsanne-led with Roussanne, Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette. Ours is the 2016, apricot, honey, fennel and herbs.

card.front: Why does Trévallon not use its local appellation?
card.back: Its founder chose grapes the rules did not allow, so it labels as Alpilles, yet it is among the south's most sought-after wines.

components.name: Château d'Esclans and Whispering Angel
components.explain:
Château d'Esclans is an estate in the hills of Provence behind the Riviera. It was bought in 2006 by a new owner whose aim was to make the greatest rosés in the world, and its Whispering Angel became the best-known pale Provence rosé in America, credited with starting a rosé boom.

The name came by chance. In the château's chapel, above the altar, is a carving of two cherubs that seemed to be whispering to each other; the label carries a line drawing of them. The estate is now part of LVMH.

Ours is the 2024: Grenache-led with Cinsault and Rolle, white peach, wild strawberry and citrus, dry and mineral.

card.front: Where does the name Whispering Angel come from?
card.back: A carving of two cherubs above the altar in Château d'Esclans' chapel that seemed to whisper. The label shows them.

items: Château d’Esclans ‘Whispering Angel’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024

components.name: Château Minuty
components.explain:
Château Minuty stands at Gassin, on the hills above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, with vineyards around Gassin and Ramatuelle looking out to sea. Gabriel Farnet bought the estate in 1936, and it has stayed with his descendants, the Matton family, ever since.

In 1955 it was named one of the crus classés of the Côtes de Provence, and today its rosés, built on Grenache, are poured all over the world.

Our glass is the Minuty Prestige 2024: pale, dry, white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest, with a light mineral finish. Sell it as a glass of the Riviera, made for the courtyard.

card.front: Where is Château Minuty, and who runs it?
card.back: At Gassin above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, held by the Farnet and Matton family since 1936. Its Prestige is our rosé by the glass.

components.name: Trimbach of Ribeauvillé
components.explain:
Trimbach is one of the oldest family wine houses in Alsace, founded in 1626 by Jean Trimbach and now in its thirteenth generation. It settled in Ribeauvillé after the First World War.

The house is famous for bone dry, high-acid, elegant whites, above all the Clos Sainte Hune, one of the world's greatest Rieslings. Its Réserve Personnelle is its top bottling of Pinot Gris, and in great years it makes late harvest wines, Vendanges Tardives.

We pour two mature Trimbach wines from 2007: the Pinot Gris Réserve Personnelle, dried apricot, honey, smoke and ginger, and the Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives, sweet with lychee, rose and cinnamon. Their sweetness levels are for the sommelier to confirm.

card.front: How old is the Trimbach house, and what is it famous for?
card.back: Founded in 1626, now in its thirteenth generation at Ribeauvillé: bone dry, elegant Alsace whites. We pour its Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer from 2007.

components.name: Joh. Jos. Prüm and the sundial
components.explain:
The Wehlener Sonnenuhr, the Wehlen sundial, is one of the Mosel's most famous vineyards, a steep slope of grey Devonian slate facing south across the river. In 1842 Jodocus Prüm, a vineyard owner, built a large sundial into the rock so the workers on the slope could tell the time, and the vineyard took its name.

The Prüm family has been in Wehlen for centuries; the Joh. Jos. Prüm estate dates from 1911, when the family's holdings were divided. Its Rieslings are delicate, lightly sweet and famously long-lived, sometimes with a little spritz when young.

We pour the Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett 2020 and the gold capsule Auslese 2015 in magnum.

card.front: How did the Wehlener Sonnenuhr get its name?
card.back: Jodocus Prüm built a sundial into its slate in 1842 so vineyard workers could tell the time. We pour Joh. Jos. Prüm's Kabinett and Auslese from it.

items: J.J. Prüm ‘Wehlener Sonnenuhr’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2015 (1.5 L magnum)

components.name: Egon Müller and the Scharzhofberg
components.explain:
The Scharzhofberg is a steep slate hill above the Saar, the coolest corner of the Mosel. For centuries it belonged to a monastery in Trier. When the French revolutionary armies seized church land, the vineyard was sold at auction in 1797 to Jean-Jacques Koch, and it passed to the Müller family through his daughter's marriage.

The family's estate, the Scharzhof, is now perhaps the most sought-after Riesling estate in Germany, and its wines were served at the royal courts of Europe. Its Kabinett is lightly sweet and low in alcohol, with an electric acidity that makes it feel weightless.

Ours is the Scharzhofberger Kabinett 2020. Present it as one of the most famous Rieslings in the world.

card.front: How did the Müller family come to own the Scharzhofberg?
card.back: It was church land sold at auction in 1797 after the French Revolution; it passed to the Müller family by marriage. Our Kabinett 2020 is from there.

components.name: Dönnhoff of the Nahe
components.explain:
Dönnhoff is a family estate at Oberhausen on the Nahe and the region's most famous grower, the name that made the world notice the Nahe.

Its vineyards include the Brücke, a tiny parcel beside the old bridge over the river that the family owns alone, and a share of the Hermannshöhle in Niederhausen, a steep slope under a cliff often called the Nahe's greatest vineyard. Its Rieslings are known for purity, precision and a smoky, stony edge.

We pour two gold capsule Auslesen from 2023 in half-bottles: the Oberhäuser Brücke, lemon curd, peach and honey, and the Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle, peach, honey and stone. Sweet, concentrated and piercing: the Riesling for fruit desserts.

card.front: What are Dönnhoff's two Auslesen on our list?
card.back: Gold capsule Auslesen from the Brücke, a tiny parcel it owns alone by the old bridge, and from the Hermannshöhle, the Nahe's greatest vineyard.

items: Dönnhoff ‘Oberhäuser Brücke’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2023 (375 ml)
Dönnhoff ‘Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2023 (375 ml)

components.name: The Mosel family estates: Berres, Dr. Hermann and Stein
components.explain:
Three small Mosel family estates give us some of our most useful Rieslings.

C.H. Berres is at Ürzig in the Middle Mosel, from a family with roots to 1510; its off-dry Old Vines is our Riesling by the glass. Weingut Dr. Hermann is a family estate at Erden, next door; its Erdener Prälat Auslese 2014 half-bottle pours by the glass with dessert, and its Würzgarten Kranklei Spätlese comes from the red slate spice garden of Ürzig. Weingut Stein is a small estate at Alf run by a grower who has rescued steep slate terraces others abandoned; we pour his Weihwasser and Palmberg-Terrassen.

Three families, steep slate, and Riesling for every course.

card.front: Which Mosel family makes our Riesling by the glass?
card.back: C.H. Berres of Ürzig, a family with roots to 1510. Dr. Hermann of Erden and Stein of Alf are our other Mosel families.

items: Dr. Hermann ‘Erdener Prälat’ Riesling Auslese 2014 (375 ml)
Dr. Hermann ‘Ürziger Würzgarten in der Kranklei’ Riesling Spätlese Goldkapsel 2018

components.name: Weingut Keller
components.explain:
Weingut Keller is a family estate at Flörsheim-Dalsheim in Rheinhessen, and one of the most admired growers in Germany. It helped show that Rheinhessen, long known for cheap, sweet wine, has limestone hills capable of greatness.

The family is best known for powerful dry Rieslings, but in good years it also makes sweet wines from late harvest and botrytis grapes.

Our bottle is its PIUS Auslese 2022 in a half-bottle, a sweet blend whose grape varieties change with the vintage: honeyed apricot, pineapple and spice, rich and pure, with Keller's stony acidity. Keller wines are rare; treat it as a find.

card.front: Why is Weingut Keller admired, and what do we pour?
card.back: It helped prove Rheinhessen's limestone can be great. We pour its PIUS Auslese, a sweet blend whose grapes change by vintage.

components.name: Bründlmayer, Loimer and Hirtzberger
components.explain:
Our Austrian wines come from three family estates on the Danube.

Bründlmayer is the leading family estate of Langenlois in the Kamptal, and the best-known grower of the Heiligenstein, the famous steep hill above Zöbing. We pour its Terrassen and Alte Reben Grüner Veltliner and its Heiligenstein Riesling. Loimer, also of Langenlois, makes Lois, a light, fresh Grüner built for food.

Franz Hirtzberger is a family estate in Spitz, at the western end of the Wachau, and Honivogl is its most famous Grüner Veltliner vineyard; ours is a Smaragd, the ripest dry category.

Light and crisp, or full and powerful: all dry, all made with food in mind.

card.front: Which Austrian families make our Grüner Veltliner wines?
card.back: Bründlmayer and Loimer of Langenlois in the Kamptal, and Franz Hirtzberger of Spitz in the Wachau, whose Honivogl is a Smaragd.

components.name: Kracher of Illmitz
components.explain:
Kracher is a family estate at Illmitz, between the village and the shore of the Neusiedlersee in Burgenland. Its vineyards sit among the lake's reeds and pools, where autumn mist brings noble rot almost every year.

Alois Kracher made it world famous from the late 1980s until his early death in 2007, with numbered collections of sweet wines that stood beside Sauternes and Tokaji; the family carries the estate on.

Ours is the Cuvée Auslese 2017, Welschriesling and Chardonnay made sweet and kept in steel: pear, quince, mandarin, passion fruit and orange blossom honey. Lighter than a Sauternes, it is lovely with fruit desserts.

card.front: What made Kracher famous?
card.back: Alois Kracher's sweet wines from the Neusiedlersee, where mist brings noble rot almost every year. We pour its Cuvée Auslese 2017.

components.name: Pazo das Bruxas: the manor of the witches
components.explain:
Pazo das Bruxas is Galician for the manor of the witches. Galicia has a rich folklore of witches, meigas, and spells, and the name plays on it.

The wine is made by Familia Torres, one of Spain's great family wine companies, better known for its Catalan wines, at its estate in Rías Baixas: Albariño, unoaked and bottled young for freshness, with lemon, white peach and a saline, sea-spray snap.

With our Barbera, Le Masche, named for the spirits said to guard its vineyard, it makes two glasses with a spell on the list. Sell it for oysters, crab claws and Gulf fish.

card.front: What does Pazo das Bruxas mean, and who makes it?
card.back: The manor of the witches, in Galician. Familia Torres makes it in Rías Baixas: unoaked Albariño, lemon and sea spray.

components.name: La Rioja Alta and the 904
components.explain:
La Rioja Alta S.A. was founded on 10 July 1890 by five families in the station quarter of Haro. In 1904 it merged with Alfredo Ardanza's winery, and to mark it the house made a Reserva 1904, which became the Gran Reserva 904. Its other great label, the 890, marks the founding year; the first digit is dropped so no one mistakes the name for a vintage.

The house is one of the great traditionalists of Rioja, ageing its wines for years in American oak barrels made in its own cooperage.

Ours is the 904 from 2015: about nine parts Tempranillo to one of Graciano, silky and savoury, dried cherry, tobacco, vanilla and leather.

card.front: What does 904 mean on the La Rioja Alta label?
card.back: It marks the 1904 merger with Ardanza's winery, with the first digit dropped so it is not read as a vintage. Ours is the 2015.

components.name: La Miraja and Le Masche
components.explain:
La Miraja is a small Piemontese producer that works from the old castle cellars of Castagnole Monferrato, in the hills of Asti.

Its Barbera d'Asti is called Le Masche, after the masche, the witches or spirits of Piemontese folklore, said to watch over the vineyard. The producer describes native fermentation in steel and about a year in neutral oak; confirm this bottle with the sommelier.

It is our Barbera by the glass: dark cherry and plum, bright acidity, soft tannin. With the Albariño from the manor of the witches, it is one of two glasses on our list that carry a spell, a fun line for guests.

card.front: What are the masche of our Barbera's name?
card.back: Spirits or witches of Piemontese folklore said to guard the vineyard. La Miraja makes Le Masche from castle cellars at Castagnole Monferrato.

components.name: Giuseppe Quintarelli
components.explain:
Giuseppe Quintarelli, called Bepi, was the great traditionalist of Valpolicella. The family estate in the hills above Negrar dates from 1924, and he ran it from the early 1950s until his death in 2012, making Amarone and Recioto that became benchmarks.

He dried his grapes for months on racks and in crates, aged the wines for years in large old casks, and refused to release them in vintages he thought unworthy. His handwritten labels became famous. His family carries the estate on in the same spirit.

Our Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997 is a rare chance: twenty-nine years old, dark cherry, fig, raisin and chocolate, sweet and velvety. A collector's bottle for chocolate desserts.

card.front: Who was Giuseppe Quintarelli?
card.back: The great traditionalist of Valpolicella, working above Negrar until 2012, famous for patient Amarone and Recioto. Ours is his 1997 Recioto.

items: Giuseppe Quintarelli Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997

components.name: Château d'Yquem
components.explain:
Château d'Yquem is the most famous sweet wine in the world. In the 1855 classification of Sauternes it was ranked alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, above every other estate.

The Lur-Saluces family held it from 1785 for more than two centuries. Thomas Jefferson, then the American minister in France, ordered it for himself and for George Washington. It now belongs to LVMH.

Yquem picks berry by berry as noble rot strikes, often in many passes through the vineyard, and in poor years makes no Yquem at all. We pour it in three vintages: 2015 and 2016 in half-bottles, and 2007 by the bottle. Honey, apricot, candied orange and saffron, and an endless finish.

card.front: What rank did Yquem receive in 1855, and which president's friend ordered it?
card.back: Premier Cru Supérieur, alone above all Sauternes. Thomas Jefferson ordered it for himself and George Washington. We pour three vintages.

components.name: Château Suduiraut
components.explain:
Château Suduiraut is a first growth of Sauternes in the village of Preignac, its vineyards next door to Château d'Yquem. Its classical château and gardens are among the grandest in the region, and it is now owned by AXA Millésimes.

Its Sauternes is Sémillon-led with a little Sauvignon Blanc, made from noble rot grapes and aged in oak: honey, apricot, candied orange, crème brûlée and vanilla, rich and luscious with fresh acidity.

We pour the 2016 in a half-bottle and the 2010 by the bottle. Sell Suduiraut as Yquem's neighbour: great Sauternes at a gentler price.

card.front: Why is Suduiraut called Yquem's neighbour?
card.back: Its vineyards in Preignac lie next to Yquem. A first growth of Sauternes: we pour the 2016 half-bottle and the 2010.

items: Château Suduiraut Sauternes Premier Cru Classé 2010

components.name: Château Climens, the Lord of Barsac
components.explain:
Château Climens is a first growth of Barsac in the 1855 classification, sometimes called the Lord of Barsac. It is unusual in making its sweet wine from Sémillon alone, from vines on limestone, and in farming biodynamically.

The Lurton family owned it from the 1970s until 2022, when a majority stake passed to a new family owner. Its wines are known for freshness and elegance rather than sheer weight, the mark of Barsac's limestone.

Ours is the 2010: candied lemon, apricot, pineapple, honey and saffron, sweet and rich with Barsac's freshness. Lovely with the citrus and caramel desserts.

card.front: What makes Château Climens unusual?
card.back: It makes Barsac from Sémillon alone, on limestone, farmed biodynamically: sweet but notably fresh. A first growth of 1855; ours is the 2010.

items: Château Climens Barsac Premier Cru Classé 2010

components.name: Château Gilette: Sauternes held back
components.explain:
Château Gilette is a tiny estate of about four and a half hectares at Preignac, run by the Médeville family. It does something no other Sauternes does: it ages its finest wine, the Crème de Tête, for close to twenty years in small concrete vats, never in oak, and releases it twenty years or more after the harvest.

The idea goes back to the family's habit of leaving the wine untouched in the vats for years, and the result is Sauternes of remarkable freshness for its age.

Ours is the 1989, thirty-seven years on: amber gold, crème brûlée, caramel, dried apricot, orange peel and saffron. A wine older than many of our guests, served with care.

card.front: What is unusual about Château Gilette's Crème de Tête?
card.back: It ages close to twenty years in small concrete vats, never oak, and is released two decades after harvest. Ours is the 1989.

components.name: Pichon Lalande and the Comtesse
components.explain:
Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande, Pichon Lalande for short, is a second growth of Pauillac, across the road from Château Latour. It was once part of one great Pichon estate, divided among the family in 1850; this share was run by Virginie, the Comtesse de Lalande, and still carries her title.

The Miailhe family bought it in 1925, and its later owner sold it in January 2007 to the family behind Champagne Louis Roederer.

It is known for using more Merlot than its neighbours, which gives it a silky, perfumed elegance. Ours is the 2004, twenty-two years on: cassis, cedar, tobacco and dried rose, with silky tannin. Decant it gently.

card.front: Who was the Comtesse in Pichon Lalande's name?
card.back: Virginie, Comtesse de Lalande, who ran her share after the Pichon estate was divided in 1850. Champagne Roederer's owners bought it in 2007.

items: Château Pichon-Longueville Comtesse de Lalande Pauillac 2ème Cru Classé 2004

components.name: Château Talbot and the English commander
components.explain:
Château Talbot, a fourth growth of Saint-Julien, is named for John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, the English commander killed at the Battle of Castillon in 1453, the battle that ended three centuries of English rule in Bordeaux. Shakespeare put him on stage.

The estate has belonged to the Cordier family since 1918 and covers about a hundred hectares of gravel near the Gironde. Its wine is classic Saint-Julien: blackcurrant, plum, cedar and cigar box, firm but fine.

Ours is the 2019. It is a good story for the table: the claret the English lost, named for the man who lost it.

card.front: Who is Château Talbot named after?
card.back: John Talbot, the English commander killed at Castillon in 1453, ending English rule in Bordeaux. A fourth growth of Saint-Julien.

components.name: Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste
components.explain:
Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste is a fifth growth of the 1855 classification in Pauillac, on a gravel rise, a puy, inland from the river. It is owned by the Borie family, a name well known in Saint-Julien and Pauillac.

It makes classic, Cabernet-led Pauillac that ages beautifully, and sommeliers often call it one of the best values in the Médoc: a fifth growth that drinks above its rank.

Ours is the 2008, eighteen years on: blackcurrant turning to cassis and cedar, tobacco, earth and graphite, the tannin now resolved. A splendid, mature claret for the Chateaubriand or the filet.

card.front: Why is Grand-Puy-Lacoste called a great value?
card.back: A fifth growth of Pauillac, owned by the Borie family, that drinks above its rank. Our 2008 is mature, cedar and cassis.

components.name: Château d'Issan and Moulin d'Issan
components.explain:
Château d'Issan is one of the oldest estates in Margaux, a moated castle in the Médoc. Over its door is carved its motto, Regum mensis arisque deorum, for the tables of kings and the altars of the gods, and the house tells that wine from its land was poured at the wedding of Eleanor of Aquitaine and Henry Plantagenet in 1152: a legend, and told as one.

Moulin d'Issan, our Bordeaux Supérieur by the glass, is made by the d'Issan team from vineyards on lower ground outside the Margaux appellation, and named for a ruined seventeenth century windmill. It is a Cabernet blend, aged partly in new barrels: cassis, plum and cedar, with polished tannin.

card.front: What is the motto over Château d'Issan's door?
card.back: For the tables of kings and the altars of the gods. The d'Issan team make our Moulin d'Issan, named for an old windmill.

components.name: Graham's, Dow's and the Symington family
components.explain:
In 1882 a young Scot, Andrew James Symington, sailed to Porto to work for the Graham family's Port house. He became a partner in Warre's and, in 1912, in Dow's, and in 1970 his grandsons bought Graham's. The Symington family now runs Graham's, Dow's, Warre's and Cockburn's, four of the great names of Port.

The houses keep distinct styles: Graham's rich and ripe, built on its Quinta dos Malvedos, bought in 1890; Dow's on the drier side of Port.

On our list: Dow's 2000 in a half-bottle, Graham's 2000 and Graham's 1983. Comparing Dow's and Graham's from the same year is a lesson in house style.

card.front: Which family owns Graham's and Dow's, and how do they differ?
card.back: The Symington family. Graham's is rich and ripe; Dow's is on the drier side. We pour both from 2000, and Graham's 1983.

components.name: Taylor Fladgate and Quinta de Vargellas
components.explain:
Taylor Fladgate is one of the oldest Port houses, its story beginning in 1692 with an English merchant, Job Bearsley. Its vintage Ports are among the most prized and long-lived of all.

In 1893 it bought Quinta de Vargellas, a great estate in the wild Douro Superior that gives the backbone of its vintage Ports. In good years when the house does not declare a full vintage, it bottles Vargellas on its own as a single quinta Vintage Port.

We pour two: the Taylor Fladgate Vintage Port 1977, a declared year, forty-nine years old, and the Quinta de Vargellas 1987, thirty-nine years old. Both are mature, refined and must be decanted.

card.front: When does Taylor's bottle Quinta de Vargellas on its own?
card.back: In good years when no full vintage is declared. Vargellas, bought in 1893, is the backbone of its Vintage Ports.

items: Taylor Fladgate ‘Quinta de Vargellas’ Vintage Port 1987

components.name: Niepoort
components.explain:
Niepoort is a family Port house of Dutch origin, founded in Vila Nova de Gaia in 1842 and still run by the same family. Small beside the big British houses, it is famous above all for its Colheitas, single-harvest tawny Ports aged for decades in cask, and lately for its Douro table wines.

We pour two very different wines from Niepoort. The Colheita 1997 in a half-bottle is a tawny, amber, with walnut, caramel, dried orange peel and coffee; it needs no decanting. The Vintage Port 1987 is a ruby style bottled young and aged in bottle, thirty-nine years on, dried cherry, fig and cocoa, and must be decanted.

One house, both great families of Port.

card.front: What is Niepoort famous for, and what two styles do we pour?
card.back: A Dutch-origin family Port house founded in 1842, famous for Colheitas. We pour its Colheita 1997 tawny and its Vintage Port 1987.

components.name: Sandeman's Don and Feist
components.explain:
Sandeman was founded in London in 1790 by George Sandeman, a Scot, who borrowed money from his father to ship Port and sherry. In 1928 an artist drew the Don, a caped figure in a Portuguese student's cape and a Spanish hat, holding a glass of wine; it is called the oldest wine logo still in use, and it is on our bottle.

Feist is an old Port house founded by two German cousins and now part of the Sogevinus group, best known for ruby and tawny Ports.

Both of ours are Late Bottled Vintage Ports with long bottle age: Sandeman 1999 and Feist 2006, dark cherry, plum, fig and cocoa. Show guests the Don on the label.

card.front: Who is the caped figure on the Sandeman bottle?
card.back: The Don, drawn in 1928 and called the oldest wine logo still in use. Sandeman was founded in London in 1790.

components.name: Inniskillin and Canadian icewine
components.explain:
Inniskillin was founded on the Niagara Peninsula of Ontario in 1975, with the first new winery licence granted there since Prohibition, as the house tells it. Its founders, an Austrian-born winemaker and a Canadian nurseryman, set out to make Canadian icewine on European lines.

The world took notice in 1991, when Inniskillin's Vidal Icewine 1989 won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux, the moment Canadian icewine arrived.

Ours is a rare red icewine from Cabernet Franc, the 2015: grapes picked frozen in a Canadian winter, pressed while still frozen, giving strawberry, raspberry, rhubarb and candied fruit, intensely sweet with vivid acidity.

card.front: What put Inniskillin and Canadian icewine on the map?
card.back: Its Vidal Icewine 1989 won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in 1991. We pour its rare red Cabernet Franc icewine.

items: Inniskillin Cabernet Franc Icewine Niagara Peninsula 2015

components.name: Inglenook and Rubicon
components.explain:
Inglenook was founded at Rutherford in 1879 by Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain who had made his fortune in the Alaska trade, and it became one of Napa's first great estates.

Its vineyards were later split up and the famous name sold off. In 1975 a film-making family bought part of the old estate with proceeds from a hit film, and from the 1978 harvest made Rubicon, a Cabernet Sauvignon-led blend with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot, named for Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon. Over the years they reunited the estate, and in 2011 bought back the Inglenook name.

We pour Rubicon 2010 by the glass at $70, sixteen years old: blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth.

card.front: Who founded Inglenook, and what is Rubicon named for?
card.back: Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain, in 1879. Rubicon, first made in 1978, is named for Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon.

components.name: Paul Hobbs and Coombsville
components.explain:
Paul Hobbs founded his own winery in 1991 at Sebastopol in Sonoma County, after years making wine for others in California and South America. He is known for single-vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay made with a light hand.

His Napa estate is in Coombsville, one of the valley's cooler corners in the hills east of the city of Napa, and is named for Nathan Coombs, the man who founded the city. Its Cabernet ripens slowly, keeping freshness alongside Napa's dark fruit.

Our dinner tasting pours the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 with the Rohan duck: dark fruit, cocoa and firm structure. It is young, so it is opened or decanted ahead.

card.front: Which Napa Cabernet pours on the dinner tasting, and with what?
card.back: Paul Hobbs Coombsville 2021, from one of Napa's cooler corners, with the Rohan duck. Opened or decanted ahead, as it is young.

components.name: The Judgment of Paris
components.explain:
On 24 May 1976, a British wine merchant in Paris held a blind tasting of top California and French wines, judged by leading French experts, to mark America's bicentennial. Everyone expected France to win.

Instead the Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay from Calistoga came first among the whites, ahead of great white Burgundies, and a Napa Cabernet won the reds. Its winemaker then was Mike Grgich, who went on to found Grgich Hills in Rutherford. Ridge's Monte Bello 1971 came fifth among the reds, and in the thirtieth anniversary re-tasting in 2006 it came first.

Our Montelena Chardonnay, the Grgich Hills Violetta and the Ridge Estate Cabernet all trace back to that afternoon, when the world took California seriously.

card.front: Which wine won the whites at the Judgment of Paris in 1976?
card.back: Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay, made by Mike Grgich, beating top white Burgundy. Ridge Monte Bello won the 2006 re-tasting thirty years later.

items: Grgich Hills ‘Violetta’ Late Harvest Napa Valley 2012 (375 ml)
Ridge Vineyards ‘Estate’ Cabernet Sauvignon Santa Cruz Mountains 2020 (375 ml)

components.name: Ridge Vineyards
components.explain:
Ridge Vineyards began high in the Santa Cruz Mountains at Monte Bello, whose Cabernet won the 2006 re-tasting of the Judgment of Paris. It is also America's great champion of old-vine Zinfandel.

Since 1972 it has made Lytton Springs from old vines in Sonoma's Dry Creek Valley, a field blend planted from 1901 with Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Carignane and more, and it bought the vineyard in the early 1990s. Ridge prints every grape and every winemaking step on its back labels, a habit sommeliers love.

We pour five: Lytton Springs in two vintages, Three Valleys, the Estate Cabernet half-bottle, and Essence, a rare late harvest Zinfandel made only when the grapes can hang long enough.

card.front: What is Ridge known for besides Monte Bello?
card.back: Old-vine Zinfandel field blends such as Lytton Springs, made since 1972, and for back labels listing every grape and every step.

items: Ridge Vineyards ‘Lytton Springs’ Dry Creek Valley 2021 (375 ml)
Ridge Vineyards ‘Estate’ Cabernet Sauvignon Santa Cruz Mountains 2020 (375 ml)

components.name: Duckhorn Vineyards
components.explain:
Duckhorn Vineyards was founded in 1976 in St. Helena, in the heart of the Napa Valley, by Dan and Margaret Duckhorn. Its first vintage, in 1978, included a Merlot from the Three Palms Vineyard, and Duckhorn became famous for Merlot at a time when few in America took the grape seriously; the Three Palms Merlot was Wine Spectator's Wine of the Year in 2017.

Today it makes Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc as well as Merlot.

We pour two: the Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon 2022, ripe and structured with blackberry, cassis and cedar, and the North Coast Sauvignon Blanc half-bottle, crisp with grapefruit and melon.

card.front: What grape made Duckhorn famous?
card.back: Merlot: its first vintage in 1978 included a Three Palms Merlot. We pour its Napa Cabernet and its North Coast Sauvignon Blanc.

items: Duckhorn Sauvignon Blanc North Coast 2023 (375 ml)

components.name: Chateau Montelena
components.explain:
Chateau Montelena is a stone château at the foot of Mount Saint Helena in Calistoga, at the northern end of the Napa Valley, built in the late nineteenth century. Its 1973 Chardonnay beat the best of Burgundy at the Paris tasting of 1976, a story later told in a Hollywood film.

The house style for Chardonnay is balanced and restrained, made without the full malolactic richness many Napa Chardonnays have, so it keeps bright acidity and green apple freshness.

Ours is the Napa Valley Chardonnay 2023: green apple, lemon, pear and a little toast. Say it to the guest who loves Burgundy but wants California: the Chardonnay that beat France.

card.front: Why is Chateau Montelena Chardonnay famous?
card.back: Its 1973 beat top white Burgundy at the 1976 Paris tasting. It is made restrained, without full malolactic richness, so it stays bright.

components.name: Grgich Hills and Violetta
components.explain:
Grgich Hills Estate in Rutherford was founded by Mike Grgich, the winemaker, born in Croatia, who made the Chateau Montelena Chardonnay that won the Paris tasting of 1976. He went on to found his own estate, known for Chardonnay and Cabernet, with its own vineyards farmed organically.

In rare years, when noble rot touches the grapes, Grgich Hills makes a late harvest dessert wine called Violetta: Sauvignon Blanc with Riesling and Gewürztraminer, sweet and luscious, with dried peach, candied orange, honey and sweet flowers.

Ours is the 2012 in a half-bottle. Pour small, well chilled, with fruit desserts and the Baked Apple.

card.front: Who founded Grgich Hills, and what is Violetta?
card.back: Mike Grgich, winemaker of the 1976 Paris-winning Montelena Chardonnay. Violetta is its rare late harvest dessert wine, touched by noble rot.

items: Grgich Hills ‘Violetta’ Late Harvest Napa Valley 2012 (375 ml)

components.name: Kongsgaard
components.explain:
Kongsgaard is a small family winery in the Napa Valley whose Chardonnays are among the most sought after in California, made in small amounts.

The style is rich and layered yet fresh, from patient cellar work and long ageing in barrel, and the wines are built to age in bottle like great white Burgundy.

Ours is the 2016, ten years on: lemon curd, baked pear, hazelnut, honey and a smoky, savoury depth, with a very long finish. It is a cult bottle for a guest who knows California, and a splendid match for lobster and rich crab dishes.

card.front: What kind of wine is our Kongsgaard?
card.back: A cult Napa Chardonnay from a small family winery, rich yet fresh and built to age. Our 2016 has a decade in bottle.

components.name: Au Bon Climat, Sandhi and Gainey
components.explain:
Three Santa Barbara County producers on our list show how the Sta. Rita Hills turned California Chardonnay towards freshness.

Au Bon Climat, founded by the late Jim Clendenen, was a pioneer of Burgundian-style Chardonnay in the county; ours comes from the historic Sanford & Benedict vineyard, one of the oldest in the hills. Sandhi was founded by a sommelier and a winemaker known for fresh, restrained wine. Gainey Estate Vineyards, a family estate, makes our Chardonnay by the glass: lemon curd, baked apple and a creamy texture with bright acidity.

Say California fruit with Burgundian freshness: ideal for the crab, the redfish and the lobster.

card.front: Which Santa Barbara Chardonnay do we pour by the glass?
card.back: Gainey Estate Vineyards, from the cool Sta. Rita Hills. Au Bon Climat and Sandhi are our bottles from the same hills.

items: Au Bon Climat ‘Sanford & Benedict’ Chardonnay Sta. Rita Hills 2021

components.name: Bergstrom and Ken Wright
components.explain:
Two Willamette Valley families make our Oregon Pinot Noir.

Bergstrom is a family winery near Newberg, known for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Its Reserve Pinot Noir half-bottle shows the valley's style: red cherry, cranberry and forest floor, fine tannin and bright acidity, more depth than its weight suggests.

Ken Wright Cellars is in Carlton, and Ken Wright is known for bottling Pinot Noir vineyard by vineyard to show each site. Our bottle is his valley-wide blend, drawn from those vineyards: young and bright, red cherry, raspberry and spice.

Say Oregon Pinot Noir: Burgundy's grape, Oregon's bright fruit, lovely with the redfish and the duck.

card.front: Which Oregon Pinot Noirs do we pour?
card.back: Bergstrom's Reserve half-bottle, from near Newberg, and Ken Wright's Willamette Valley blend, from a grower known for single-vineyard wines. Both are bright and earthy.

items: Bergstrom ‘Reserve’ Pinot Noir Willamette Valley 2022 (375 ml)
Ken Wright Cellars Willamette Valley Pinot Noir 2024

components.name: Chalk Hill and Kumeu River
components.explain:
Two Chardonnay estates, a world apart, round out our New World whites.

Chalk Hill is an estate in Sonoma County named for the Chalk Hill area in the hills east of Windsor, south-east of Healdsburg. Its Chardonnay half-bottle is creamy and round, with ripe pear, baked apple and a little toasty oak: California richness in a smaller pour.

Kumeu River, near Auckland on New Zealand's North Island, is run by the Brajkovich family and famous for Chardonnay in a Burgundian style. Its Estate is lemon, white peach and hazelnut with a fine, mineral finish.

One rich, one restrained: let the guest's taste choose.

card.front: How do Chalk Hill and Kumeu River Chardonnay differ?
card.back: Chalk Hill, from Sonoma, is creamy and round with toasty oak; Kumeu River, from near Auckland, is restrained and Burgundian.

items: Chalk Hill Chardonnay Sonoma County 2021 (375 ml)

components.name: Gaia Wines of Santorini
components.explain:
Gaia Wines makes Assyrtiko on Santorini, the volcanic island in the Aegean. Its vines are very old and ungrafted, trained low in kouloura baskets against the wind in pumice soil that phylloxera never reached.

Its Wild Ferment is named for the way it is made: fermented with the island's own native yeasts rather than added ones, and aged in a mix of steel, oak, acacia and ceramic vessels to build texture without the taste of wood.

Ours is the 2023: lemon, salt, flint and white flowers, bone dry, with piercing acidity and a savoury depth. It is the white for the grilled fish and anything with lemon and herbs.

card.front: Why is Gaia's Assyrtiko called Wild Ferment?
card.back: It is fermented with Santorini's native yeasts, not added ones, and aged in mixed vessels for texture. Bone dry, salty and electric.

components.name: Pairing past the artichoke
components.explain:
Artichokes are famously hard on wine. They contain cynarin, a compound that briefly blocks the sweet receptors on the tongue, so the next sip tastes oddly sweet or flat, and oak and tannin can turn metallic.

The answer is a bone dry, high-acid, unoaked, herbal white with little fruit sweetness to exaggerate and no oak to turn: a Loire Sauvignon Blanc is the classic. In the Eggs Sardou the crispy artichokes come with Parmesan creamed spinach and a Choron sauce in place of hollandaise, which helps further, and the tarragon in the Choron is a direct bridge to the wine's herbs.

That is why the Durand Sauvignon Blanc by the glass is the first pick with the Eggs Sardou. Say: artichokes are tricky with wine, but a Loire Sauvignon Blanc loves them.

card.front: Why is the Durand Sauvignon Blanc the pick with Eggs Sardou?
card.back: Artichokes contain cynarin, which makes most wines taste oddly sweet or metallic; a bone dry, herbal, unoaked Loire Sauvignon Blanc survives them.

components.name: The by-the-glass list
components.explain:
Brennan's pours about twenty wines by the glass, chosen to cover every course and style: the house Champagne and Rare, a Crémant rosé, the Berres Riesling, crisp and fuller whites, a Provence rosé, light and fuller reds, and dessert wines. Two are poured by Coravin, the Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé through the cork and the Rare under a sparkling stopper, so a single glass of a great wine is possible.

The live list is the Binwise page linked from the restaurant's wine menu, and it changes as the cellar changes; prices and vintages sometimes differ between the Binwise list and the printed glass page.

So the rule is simple: check the list you are handed on shift, read the label at lineup, and quote the price as printed.

card.front: Which glass pours use Coravin, and where is the live glass list?
card.back: The Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé and the Rare. The live list is the Binwise page; check the list in hand on shift and read the label at lineup.
